## Limitations and Open Problems

The central open limitation follows directly from the foundational estimator: NeRF does not evaluate a closed-form surface integral, but queries an MLP at many discrete positions along every camera ray and approximates the continuous transmittance-weighted color integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance, and identify this ray-marching workload as the reason rendering is far too slow for interactive visualization. The implication is not merely inconvenient runtime: training and inference both repeat dense neural evaluations over empty, occupied, and occluded intervals, so high visual fidelity is coupled in the original design to substantial per-pixel computation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] This cost has two distinct dimensions that should not be collapsed. Training is slow because rendered views must be generated and differentiated through many network queries before photometric gradients update the field; rendering is slow because novel pixels require the same sample-and-integrate process. Work on sampling toolboxes reports that optimizing and rendering NeRFs is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering, and that improved transmittance-estimation or sampling strategies can reduce training time across NeRF variants. Those results treat sample allocation as a systems and estimator problem, but they also show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy does not remove the underlying many-sample requirement. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

The usual acceleration response introduces a representation trade-off rather than a free improvement. Baking a NeRF into a sparse voxel grid can make rendering much faster, but SNeRG-style caching stores opacity, diffuse color, and learned features in volumetric textures; the selected MobileNeRF discussion states that this approach still ray marches through a sparse grid, cannot fully exploit commodity GPU parallelism, and needs significant GPU memory, which prevents execution on common mobile devices. Thus, replacing MLP evaluations with explicit caches may shift cost from network computation to storage, texture access, and memory bandwidth rather than eliminating resource demand. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] Hybrid encodings expose the same trade-off from another direction. Hash tables and feature grids can converge and render faster than a plain MLP because much of the scene signal is stored in shallow, local data structures, but surveys and distillation work note that these representations have less clear geometric meaning and can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing. Conversely, purely implicit MLP representations are described as comparatively convenient for some texture, lighting, deformation, stylization, and dynamic-modeling operations, while explicit or hybrid structures often train faster and support geometry-aware manipulation more directly. The open problem is therefore task-dependent deployment: compactness, editability, geometric interpretability, optimization speed, and rendering speed do not reduce to one universally dominant architecture. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:291b93a733e7]

A second foundational limitation is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only requires a field's accumulated colors and densities along rays to explain the training images; it does not require density to coincide with a unique, clean surface. Later geometry-oriented work states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable when view-dependent effects and changing lighting can be absorbed by the radiance field, and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce that effect on geometry. Consequently, a NeRF can produce convincing novel views while leaving occupancy, surface location, or the division between geometry and appearance underdetermined from the selected viewpoint and image loss alone. [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] The view-dependent color channel is both a capability and a source of this ambiguity. Letting color depend on viewing direction enables non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, but the original emitted-radiance output does not separately identify albedo, roughness, incident illumination, shadows, or inter-reflection. Methods such as NeILF add a neural incident light field and physically based inter-reflection constraints precisely to jointly estimate geometry, materials, and lighting. The need for those extra fields and constraints indicates that the foundational color-and-density representation is optimized for view synthesis, not by itself for a uniquely decomposed inverse-rendering solution. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

The discretized volume model also has approximation limits. The differentiable ray-casting exposition cited here makes the piecewise-constant assumption explicit: density and color are treated as constant around each sampled neighborhood when the continuous integral is replaced by finite alpha weights. If samples are too sparse, or the sampling distribution misses thin or high-frequency structure, the estimator can misestimate opacity and color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this by biasing later samples toward regions with visible content, but it is a heuristic allocation strategy dependent on the coarse pass; it is not an exact quadrature rule or a guarantee that all relevant geometry is sampled. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Scale and aliasing create a separate failure mode. The original point query takes a single 3D coordinate and viewing direction, so it does not explicitly encode the conical footprint or scale of a camera pixel. Mip-VoG states that NeRF yields blurred results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales and aliasing artifacts for distant test views, while Mip-NeRF addresses scale with a conical-frustum representation but remains offline because integrated positional encoding still requires MLP queries. This shows that high quality under one sampling scale does not automatically imply consistent anti-aliased rendering across resolutions or camera distances. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Static NeRF also does not solve non-rigid or topology-changing scenes. The foundational field is a static coordinate-to-color-and-density function fitted per scene. Nerfies extends it with a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation fields conditioned on latent codes for casually captured deformable scenes; HyperNeRF further argues that continuous deformation-based approaches struggle when topology changes, because a discontinuity in correspondence conflicts with a continuous deformation field, and instead lifts the radiance field into a higher-dimensional space. These extensions demonstrate that motion, changing topology, and temporal correspondence are additional assumptions outside the original static volume-rendering formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] Finally, per-scene optimization and known posed images limit the original applicability. The basic pipeline needs multiple views with camera poses and optimizes a separate network for each scene; it is not a feed-forward reconstruction model for arbitrary unseen scenes or a single-image generative model. Single-view and diffusion-based systems add learned priors or generators to fill unobserved content, while generative approaches such as Pix2NeRF may additionally be restricted to one object category per dataset. These limitations should be stated as boundaries of the foundational NeRF evidence: the differentiable renderer explains how posed multi-view images supervise a radiance field, but it does not itself supply camera localization, cross-scene generalization, priors for unseen regions, or real-time performance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471]

## Conclusion

The central answer is that NeRF is a continuous coordinate-based radiance-and-density field, not an explicit geometric cache, and its image-formation model is transmittance-weighted volume rendering along camera rays. The discrete alpha-compositing estimator makes the classical rendering integral tractable and differentiable, so multi-view RGB error can train density and color jointly without 3D labels. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The main trade-off in the foundational design is expressiveness against computation and geometric specificity. Continuous density and view-dependent color can represent occlusion, thin or semi-transparent structure, and specular appearance, but vanilla training and rendering require many MLP evaluations along rays, and convincing images do not guarantee a unique surface or a decomposition into albedo, roughness, and illumination. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] Hierarchical sampling and positional encoding are supporting components rather than replacements for the core representation: one refines where samples are placed, and the other improves high-frequency expressivity. Later grids, hash encodings, baking, rasterization, deformation, anti-aliasing, generative, and inverse-rendering methods extend or alter this pipeline under additional assumptions; their efficiency or task results should not be treated as matched measurements of original NeRF. issues.explanation: The sentence 'MobileNeRF is introduced to run on common devices' is bound only to c2 and c37. c2 is the MobileNeRF paper itself, which states 'we introduce MobileNeRF, a NeRF that can run on a variety of common devices at interactive frame rates'; c37 is the Hyb-NeRF paper. Neither source excerpt provides a direct statement that MobileNeRF is 'introduced to run on common devices' as a stated design goal; the claim is an unsupported inference from the paper's title/abstract context rather than a directly quoted or paraphrased assertion in the cited source text.

The claim 'surveys and distillation work note that these representations have less clear geometric meaning and can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing' is bound to c32, c30, and c3. c32 (PVD paper) states 'the hashtable-based representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.' c30 is the same PVD paper (s8bd7ff5657c430dbb199) but its source excerpt discusses implicit vs. explicit representation trade-offs for editing, not hash-table geometric meaning. c3 is the MobileNeRF paper (s8f1d1db7c14909f982c5), which does not discuss hash-table geometric meaning or spatial-relation-aware editing at all. The citation c3 is unsupported for this specific claim.

The sentence 'Mip-NeRF addresses scale with a conical-frustum representation but remains offline because integrated positional encoding still requires MLP queries' is bound to c24 and c15. c24 is the Mip-VoG paper (se0e76d8b04f2c0b98f85), which states 'Mip-NeRF proposes a multiscale representation as a conical frustum to encode scale information. Nevertheless, this approach is only suitable for offline rendering since it relies on integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query a multilayer perceptron (MLP).' This is a direct paraphrase and is supported. However, c15 is the original NeRF paper (sb2f03ae500627869ea69), which does not discuss Mip-NeRF, conical frustums, or integrated positional encoding. The citation c15 is unnecessary and unsupported for this specific claim about Mip-NeRF.

The sentence 'Nerfies extends it with a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation fields conditioned on latent codes for casually captured deformable scenes' is bound to c22, c25, and c36. c22 is the Nerfies paper (s8ebf02327c77828307c9), which directly supports this claim. c25 is the HyperNeRF paper (sabc3c64445b0af5300b9), which reviews NeRF foundations and mentions Nerfies as a prior method but does not provide the detailed description of Nerfies' canonical field + deformation field + latent codes. c36 is also the HyperNeRF paper (s76e3031bc2d115d9fbef), which discusses deformation-based approaches generally. The citations c25 and c36 are not necessary for this specific claim about Nerfies' architecture; they are tangential references rather than direct support.

The sentence 'Later grids, hash encodings, baking, rasterization, deformation, anti-aliasing, generative, and inverse-rendering methods extend or alter this pipeline under additional assumptions' is bound to 12 citations (c5, c15, c26, c37, c2, c19, c32, c22, c36, c24, c17, c8). While each individual method category has some support among these citations, the conclusion unit packs a very broad enumeration of method types with a dense citation list. Several citations (e.g., c5 for volume ray casting, c15 for original NeRF, c8 for original NeRF) are not directly about 'later extensions' but about the foundational method itself, creating a mismatch between the claim ('later methods extend or alter') and some of the cited sources (which describe the original method, not extensions).

claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.
RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.

RayGauss provides a physically consistent formulation of emitted radiance c and density σ, decomposed with Gaussian functions associated with Spherical Gaussians/Harmonics for all-frequency colorimetric representation.
RayGauss introduces a method enabling differentiable ray casting of irregularly distributed Gaussians using an algorithm that integrates radiance fields slab by slab and leverages a BVH structure.
RayGauss achieves superior rendering quality compared to the state-of-the-art while maintaining reasonable training times.

RayGauss proposes a novel definition of radiance fields based on their decomposition into a weighted sum of locally supported elliptical basis functions with optimizable positions, orientations, and scales.

RayGauss associates a combination of spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG) with elliptical basis functions to better represent high-frequency color variations such as specular reflections.
RayGauss uses volume ray casting, which produces high-quality images with fewer simplifications than splatting-based methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Splatting algorithms simplify the scene using multiple approximations, allowing faster rendering but causing many artifacts when deviating from the training views, such as flickering due to a sudden change in primitives ordering.

RayGauss introduces a ray casting algorithm for sparse basis functions that sequentially integrates the radiance field slab-by-slab, accumulating colorimetric properties along the ray in slabs of space corresponding to multiple samples.

claim_records.text: NeRFMeshing proposes a novel compact and flexible architecture that enables easy 3D surface reconstruction from any NeRF-driven approach.
NeRFMeshing distills the volumetric 3D representation of a trained radiance field into a Signed Surface Approximation Network, allowing easy extraction of the 3D mesh and appearance.

fact_fields.method: NeRFMeshing distillation into Signed Surface Approximation Network

claim_records.text: The final 3D mesh produced by NeRFMeshing is physically accurate and can be rendered in real time on an array of devices.
NeRFMeshing is an end-to-end pipeline for efficiently extracting geometrically accurate meshes from trained NeRF-based networks, merely adding a very small overhead in time.
NeRFMeshing produces meshes with neural colors having accurate geometry that can be rendered in real time on commodity hardware.

NeRFMeshing introduces a novel signed surface approximation network (SSAN) that produces an accurate 3D triangle mesh of the scene rendered using a small appearance network to produce view-dependent colors.
In contrast to other works that leverage distance fields requiring significant modifications in the used NeRF architecture, NeRFMeshing can be leveraged together with any NeRF.

SSAN estimates a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) and a feature appearance field, harnessing the NeRF approximated geometry as well as the used training views to distill the trained NeRF into the SSAN model.
The 3D mesh extracted from the trained SSAN can be rendered on embedded devices at high frame-rate using rasterization and the appearance network.
NeRFMeshing does not rely on a fixed grid template during training, enabling reconstruction at any arbitrary resolution afterwards.
NeRFMeshing does not require any changes to the NeRF architecture in order to compute a surface.

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF represents the NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

MobileNeRF renders polygons with a z-buffer to produce an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color.

fact_fields.method: Traditional polygon rasterization with z-buffer plus fragment shader MLP

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF achieves interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones, by using the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline which provides massive pixel-level parallelism.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG's precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.
SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce features for each pixel, and thus cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity GPUs.

fact_fields.method: SNeRG rendering via ray marching through sparse voxel grid

claim_records.text: SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.
MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling it to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF surface texture storage vs volumetric texture storage

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that allows any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.
PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations, from shallower to deeper, to enable fast conversions.
PVD employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem.
Empirical validation of PVD is conducted on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model can be distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model at a 10X~20X faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.
PVD empowers downstream applications to optimally adapt neural representations for the task at hand in a post hoc fashion.

A NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality and reduces training time compared to a NeRF trained from scratch using 25 hours on the Family and Barn scene from the TanksAndTemples dataset.
TensoRF leverages VM (vector-matrix) decomposition and canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) to produce compact feature tensor representations.
Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (INGP) utilizes multilevel hash tables for effective compression of feature tensors.
Implicit NeRF representations make texture editing of scenes (such as color, lighting changes and deformations) easier, to the extent of artistic stylization and dynamic scene modeling.

Methods with explicit or hybrid NeRF representations usually enjoy faster training due to shallower representations and cope better with geometric-aware editing like merging and other manipulations of scenes.
PVD offers any-to-any conversion between possibly heterogeneous NeRF architectures by first constructing a unified view of them, then employing systematic progressive distillation in multiple stages.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often either helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

When a teacher model with hash table is used to distill a student model of explicit representation, it is possible to benefit from the faster training speed of the teacher while still producing a student model with clear geometric structures.

PVD offers any-to-any conversion between possibly heterogeneous NeRF architectures by first constructing a unified view of them, then employing systematic progressive distillation in multiple stages.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often either helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

When a teacher model with hash table is used to distill a student model of explicit representation, it is possible to benefit from the faster training speed of the teacher while still producing a student model with clear geometric structures.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field, which is capable of creating color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF leverages an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
This survey reviews recent advances in NeRF and categorizes them according to their architectural designs, especially in the field of novel view synthesis.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI represents scenes efficiently through foreground and background decomposition, leading to 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models which heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
CAMPARI faces the challenge of generating inward-facing faces compared to the traditional inverted faces also known as the hollow face illusion where convex faces appear concave.
Pix2NeRF introduces a novel pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, building upon π-GAN, a 3D image synthesis generative model that maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, offering potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
A limitation of Pix2NeRF is its current restriction to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space for NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric field reconstruction technique is designed for volumes where multiple light scattering effects are omnipresent, such as clouds.
The unknown distribution of volumetric fields is modeled using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.
The neural diffusion model is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly, monoplanar representation.
A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space.

The proposed approach's use of a physically-based differentiable volume renderer for latent-space light transport gradients makes reconstructions better aligned with observed data, in contrast to classic NeRF approaches.

fact_fields.method: physically-based differentiable volume renderer coupled with diffusion model

claim_records.text: Experiments demonstrate single-view reconstruction of volumetric clouds at a previously unattainable quality.

Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and the presence of vanishing gradients, and this limitation can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

For complex volumetric materials such as clouds, smoke, or fire, the reconstruction problem is so ill-posed that it requires dozens, if not hundreds, of different views to adequately constrain object parameters.
Using diffusion models for single-view volume reconstruction is challenging because no publicly available 3D dataset exists on which a diffusion model can be trained.
The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR) toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR)

claim_records.text: The proposed approach includes controlled variations in the diffusion step by considering the gradient of the image loss with respect to the learned latent space representation.
The diffusion model is trained on a dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields of cumulus clouds, using a novel diffusion-friendly representation for decoding.
The reconstruction is simultaneously constrained by the diffusion prior and the image containing light transport effects.
The renderer is coupled with the diffusion model to reconstruct radiance parameters using the prior for the density distribution but not for its appearance.
The 3D density field can be trained solely on the prior, not requiring images of all possible backgrounds and light scattering effects.
The proposed key contribution includes a large database of 3D cumulus cloud-like density fields generated using numerical fluid simulation.
The proposed key contribution includes a 3D cloud decoder utilizing a novel, diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation, trained jointly on a subset of the database.

fact_fields.method: 3D cloud decoder with diffusion-friendly monoplanar representation

claim_records.text: The proposed key contribution includes a novel Parametric Diffusion Posterior Sampling (PDPS) technique utilizing a shape-centric prior with a physically-based differentiable volume renderer.
To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first approach that integrates an unconditional diffusion model trained on volumetric density distributions with a differentiable volume renderer.

fact_fields.method: unconditional diffusion model + differentiable volume renderer integration

claim_records.text: The proposed approach is demonstrated across various tasks including single- and multi-view reconstruction, and volume super-resolution.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a novel neural radiance field with a multi-resolution hybrid encoding that achieves efficient neural modeling and fast rendering, while also allowing for high-quality novel view synthesis.
Hyb-NeRF represents the scene using different encoding strategies from coarse-to-fine resolution levels.
Hyb-NeRF exploits memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions and the fast optimization speed and local details of hash-based feature grids at fine resolutions.

claim_records.text: NerfDiff distills knowledge of a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF by synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on the ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D datasets.
NerfDiff jointly trains a camera-space triplane-based NeRF together with a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) on a collection of scenes at the training stage.
A naive finetuning strategy that optimizes NeRF parameters directly using CDM outputs leads to subpar renderings because CDM outputs tend to be multi-view inconsistent.

fact_fields.method: naive NeRF finetuning using CDM outputs

claim_records.text: NerfDiff's NeRF-guided distillation updates the NeRF representation and guides the multi-view diffusion process in an alternating fashion.
NerfDiff introduces an efficient image-conditioned NeRF representation based on camera-aligned triplanes that enables efficient rendering and finetuning from the CDM.
NerfDiff's 3D-aware CDM integrates volume rendering into 2D diffusion models to facilitate generalization to novel views.
Generalizable NeRF models conditioned by projecting 3D points and gathering corresponding image features produce blurry results when target views are far from the input view.

fact_fields.method: generalizable NeRF models conditioned on projected 3D point image features

claim_records.text: Existing 2D generative model approaches for single-image view synthesis conditioned on the input view are only able to synthesize partially 3D-consistent images.
NeRF requires tens or hundreds of images for overfitting a scene and has no generalization ability to infer new scenes.

claim_records.text: EvaSurf can be trained in 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS.
The final rendering package required for EvaSurf takes up only 40-50 MB of storage.
EvaSurf employs an efficient surface-based model with a multi-view supervision module to ensure accurate mesh reconstruction.
EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf uses a lightweight neural shader paired with explicit geometry and implicit texture to reduce computation cost and support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.
EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf's training procedure is 10× faster than MobileNeRF when completed on a single GPU.
NeRF-based methods require plenty of sampling points to forward a deep MLP network, requiring massive computation that is impractical for mobile devices.

Recent Gaussian-based methods achieve high-quality rendering with high efficiency via explicit representations, but fail to render at interactive framerates on mobile devices due to large disk storage requirements and lack of mobile-end optimization.

Existing surface-based efficient rendering methods that bake implicit-explicit hybrid representations into meshes are insufficient to obtain accurate meshes with smooth and solid surfaces for complex structures or non-Lambertian surfaces, and struggle to render view-dependent effects such as specularities due to entangled appearance and material learning.
EvaSurf's two-stage framework separately reconstructs geometry and appearance to avoid entangled attributions from joint geometry and appearance learning.
EvaSurf incorporates view-aware encoding into an implicit texture to assign different weights to dimensions of the view-aware texture, modeling appearance with view-dependent effects.
EvaSurf's final rendering package storage is much smaller than existing methods including MobileNeRF and other referenced surface-based methods.

claim_records.text: NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 22.77 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 20.85.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.823 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 0.747.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.298 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 0.513.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 17.17 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 16.64.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.672 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 0.635.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.523 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 0.651.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 17.88 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 16.86.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.738 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 0.702.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.435 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 0.602.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 22.37 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 21.55.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.799 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 0.765.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.391 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 0.529.
NeRF++ uses twice the number of samples per camera ray compared to a single volume NeRF, doubling NeRF's sample count for fairness.

For outdoor 360-degree captures centered on nearby objects, the dynamic depth range can be extremely large because background elements such as buildings, mountains, and clouds can be arbitrarily far away.
NeRF++ partitions scene space into an inner unit sphere containing foreground and all cameras, and an outer volume represented by an inverted sphere covering the complement of the inner volume.

In theory, optimizing NeRF's 5D radiance function from a set of training images can encounter critical degenerate solutions that fail to generalize to novel test views in the absence of regularization.
The shape-radiance ambiguity allows fitting a set of training images perfectly for an arbitrary incorrect geometry by choosing a suitable outgoing 2D radiance at each surface point.
NeRF's specific MLP structure implicitly encodes a smooth BRDF prior on surface reflectance, which helps avoid shape-radiance ambiguity.
A shape-radiance ambiguity solution that perfectly fits training images has very limited ability to synthesize novel views unless training views are extremely dense.

claim_records.text: NeRF yields blurred rendering results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts when test images are taken from distant views.
Mip-NeRF uses a conical frustum multiscale representation with integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query an MLP, making it only suitable for offline rendering.
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture designed for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.

claim_records.text: pixelNeRF outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines for novel view synthesis and single image 3D reconstruction when demonstrated on multi-object ShapeNet scenes and real scenes from the DTU dataset.
NeRF represents a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field f that maps a 3D point x and viewing direction unit vector d to a differential density σ and RGB color c.
NeRF renders a 2D image from its volumetric radiance field via the integral Ĉ(r) = ∫_{tn}^{tf} T(t)σ(t)c(t)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫_{tn}^{t} σ(s) ds) handles occlusion.

In the single-view pixelNeRF case, for a query point x along a target camera ray with view direction d, a corresponding image feature is extracted from the feature volume W via projection and interpolation, then passed into the NeRF network along with spatial coordinates to produce volume-rendered output compared against the target pixel value.

For multi-view pixelNeRF, the query point x and view direction d are transformed into each input view i's coordinate system via x(i) = P(i)x, d(i) = R(i)d, processed independently by initial NeRF layers f1, then aggregated via average pooling ψ and passed to final layers f2 to produce predicted density and color.
pixelNeRF is applied to new scenes immediately without any test-time optimization, whereas running each of 60 NeRFs took 14 hours.
pixelNeRF's rendering time increases linearly when given more input views, similar to NeRF's slow rendering time.
pixelNeRF manually tunes ray sampling bounds tn, tf and a scale for the positional encoding, as in vanilla NeRF.
pixelNeRF's approach is bottlenecked by the availability of large-scale wide baseline multi-view datasets, limiting its applicability to datasets such as ShapeNet and DTU.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model to enable NeRF manipulation using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.

CLIP-NeRF uses a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance, achieved by performing shape conditioning via a learned deformation field applied to positional encoding and deferring color conditioning to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update latent codes to reflect targeted editing, trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to latent codes to enable editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing, evaluated via extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images.

Compared to voxel-based representations, Tetra-NeRF's tetrahedral representation provides more detail around parts of the scene likely to be close to the surface.
Compared to point-based representations, Tetra-NeRF's approach achieves better performance.

claim_records.text: UE4-NeRF partitions each large scene into different sub-NeRFs to support real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.
UE4-NeRF initializes polygonal meshes by constructing multiple regular octahedra within the scene, with vertices of the polygonal faces continuously optimized during training.
Inspired by Level of Detail (LOD) techniques, UE4-NeRF trains meshes of varying levels of detail for different observation levels.
UE4-NeRF, combined with the rasterization pipeline in Unreal Engine 4 (UE4), achieves real-time rendering of large-scale scenes at 4K resolution with a frame rate of up to 43 FPS.

claim_records.text: D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to dynamic domains, enabling reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single moving camera around the scene.

D-NeRF splits learning into two simultaneous fully-connected network stages: one encoding the scene into canonical space, and another mapping the canonical representation to the deformed scene at a particular time.

D-NeRF's Deformation Network Ψt is trained to output displacement ∆x that transforms a given 3D point x at time t to its canonical space position as x + ∆x, with the canonical scene set to t=0 such that Ψt(x,0)=0.
D-NeRF uses positional encoder γ(p)=<(sin(2^l π p), cos(2^l π p))>_{L=0}^L, with L=10 for spatial coordinate x and L=4 for view direction d and time t.
D-NeRF's Canonical Network is an MLP Ψx(x,d) that maps a 3D point x and view direction d to emitted color c and volume density σ in canonical configuration.
D-NeRF's Deformation Network is an MLP Ψt(x,t) that predicts a deformation field defining the transformation between the scene at time t and its canonical configuration.
D-NeRF can learn a volumetric density representation for continuous non-rigid scenes trained with a single view per time instant.

For D-NeRF volume rendering, the expected pixel color C(p,t) at time t is computed as C(p,t)=∫_{hn}^{hf} T(h,t)σ(p(h,t))c(p(h,t),d) dh, where p(h,t)=x(h)+Ψt(x(h,t)), [c,σ]=Ψx(p(h,t),d), and T(h,t)=exp(-∫_{hn}^h σ(p(s,t)) ds).

D-NeRF evaluation on its 8 dynamic scenes uses four metrics: Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS).
Baseline NeRF, designed for rigid scenes, fails to model dynamic scenes and converges to a blurry mean representation of all deformations.
T-NeRF baseline, which represents the scene as a 6D input (x,y,z,θ,φ,t) without intermediate canonical configuration, captures dynamics reasonably well but fails to retrieve high frequency details.
D-NeRF retains high-frequency original image details in novel views even when each deformation state is only observed from a single viewpoint.

D-NeRF learns a displacement field ∆x mapping all points x of a dynamic scene at a specific time to a common canonical configuration, with learned volume density and view-dependent radiance transferred back to input points for novel view rendering.

claim_records.text: NeRF's novel view synthesis performance drops significantly when the number of input training views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse-input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in estimated scene geometry and divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF addresses sparse-input NeRF artifacts by regularizing geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and annealing the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other single-scene optimization methods, and in many cases also outperforms conditional models extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: The proposed voxel grid optimization approach converges rapidly from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU while achieving NeRF-comparable quality.
Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows the method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality, yet it only takes about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.
The method with 160^3 dense voxels already outperforms NeRF in most cases.
Using softplus instead of ReLU is crucial to optimize voxel density directly, as it allows exploring density very close to 0.
The proposed post-activation can model (beyond) a sharp linear surface within a single grid cell.
The step-size-to-voxel-size ratio is an important hyperparameter for the speed-quality tradeoff.
Progressive scaling of voxel grid resolution in fine-stage training can improve training efficiency with slightly better rendering quality.

ProteusNeRF supports incremental guidance through user-friendly image-based edits.

ProteusNeRF reports a 10-30x speedup over concurrent work focusing on text-guided NeRF editing.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis and predicts frequency weights using the network, with pixel values computed via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in Neural Light Fields.
NeRDF achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.
NeRDF offers a better trade-off among speed, quality, and network size than existing methods.

claim_records.text: Optimizing and rendering Neural Radiance Fields is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering.
Improved sampling is generally applicable across NeRF variants under a unified concept of transmittance estimator.
NerfAcc is a Python toolbox that provides flexible APIs for incorporating advanced sampling methods into NeRF related methods.
NerfAcc can reduce the training time of several recent NeRF methods by 1.5x to 20x with minimal modifications to the existing codebase.
Highly customized NeRFs such as Instant-NGP can be implemented in native PyTorch using NerfAcc.
Recent works that include alternative sampling approaches to help accelerate NeRF methods often do not focus on the sampling approach itself.

claim_records.text: Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific and lack universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
All existing 3D representations inherently struggle with the trade-off between data complexity and fidelity.

The 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized tree-structured proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.

claim_records.text: Recent NeRF works can render detailed specular appearance of distant environment illumination but cannot synthesize consistent reflections of closer content.
Recent NeRF specular appearance techniques rely on large computationally-expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which severely limits optimization and rendering speed.

The NeRF-Casting model casts reflection rays from points along each camera ray and traces them through the NeRF representation to render feature vectors decoded into color using a small inexpensive network, instead of querying an expensive neural network for outgoing view-dependent radiance.
The NeRF-Casting model outperforms prior methods for view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects.
NeRF-Casting is the only existing NeRF method that can synthesize photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes.
NeRF-Casting requires comparable optimization time to current state-of-the-art view synthesis models.

claim_records.text: NeRF uses a neural network to encode color and density as a function of location and viewing angle, and generates novel views using volume rendering.

The Nerfies method generalizes NeRF by using a canonical NeRF model as a template for all observations, supplemented by a per-observation deformation field that warps 3D points in the observation frame into the canonical model frame.
The deformation field in Nerfies is represented as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) conditioned on a per-image learned latent code, allowing it to vary between observations.

claim_records.text: Rendering a single pixel in NeRF requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times.
NeLF renders a pixel via one single forward pass without ray-marching.
The R2L method uses a deep residual MLP network with 88 layers to effectively learn the light field.
The key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which knowledge is transferred from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation.
On synthetic scenes, the R2L method achieves 26-35x FLOPs reduction per camera ray compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the R2L method achieves 28-31x runtime speedup compared to NeRF.
On synthetic scenes, the R2L method delivers 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

claim_records.text: Images photographed from a low-light scene can hardly be used to train a NeRF model to produce high-quality results due to their low pixel intensities, heavy noise, and color distortion.
Combining existing low-light image enhancement methods with NeRF methods does not work well due to the view inconsistency caused by the individual 2D enhancement process.
The LLNeRF approach enhances scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images in an unsupervised manner.

The core of the LLNeRF approach is a decomposition of radiance field learning, which allows enhancing illumination, reducing noise and correcting distorted colors jointly with the NeRF optimization process.

The LLNeRF method is able to produce novel view images with proper lighting and vivid colors and details given a collection of camera-finished low dynamic range (8-bits/channel) images from a low-light scene.
Experiments demonstrate that the LLNeRF method outperforms existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods.

claim_records.text: Existing Human NeRF methods for reconstructing 3D humans typically rely on multiple 2D images from multi-view cameras or monocular videos captured from fixed camera views.
SHERF is the first generalizable Human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image.
SHERF extracts and encodes 3D human representations in canonical space, enabling rendering and animation from free views and poses.
SHERF uses a bank of 3D-aware hierarchical features including global, point-level, and pixel-aligned features to facilitate informative encoding of 3D human representations.
SHERF uses a feature fusion transformer to effectively integrate the 3D-aware hierarchical feature bank.

Extensive experiments on THuman, RenderPeople, ZJU_MoCap, and HuMMan datasets demonstrate that SHERF achieves state-of-the-art performance with better generalizability for novel view and pose synthesis.

claim_records.text: Existing NeRF editing work with diffusion prior struggles to synthesize reasonable geometry in completely uncovered regions, partly due to high diversity of synthetic contents from the diffusion model hindering the radiance field from converging to crisp and deterministic geometry.

claim_records.text: Applying latent diffusion models on real data often yields a textural shift incoherent to the image condition due to auto-encoding errors.
The two identified problems (poor geometry synthesis in uncovered regions and textural shift) are further reinforced with the use of pixel-distance losses.

claim_records.text: RT-NeRF is described as the first algorithm-hardware co-design acceleration of NeRF.

On the algorithm level, RT-NeRF integrates an efficient rendering pipeline that directly computes the geometry of pre-existing points to alleviate inefficiency from commonly adopted uniform point sampling in NeRF.
RT-NeRF leverages a coarse-grained view-dependent computing ordering scheme to eliminate unnecessary processing of invisible points.

The RT-NeRF hardware accelerator adopts a hybrid encoding scheme that adaptively switches between bitmap- or coordinate-based sparsity encoding formats for NeRF's sparse embeddings, aiming to maximize storage savings and reduce required DRAM accesses while supporting efficient NeRF decoding.

claim_records.text: The RT-NeRF hardware accelerator integrates both a dual-purpose bi-direction adder & search tree and a high-density sparse search unit to coordinate the two aforementioned encoding formats.

claim_records.text: Compared to Nerfies, HyperNeRF reduces average error rates by 4.1% for the interpolation task as measured by LPIPS.
Compared to Nerfies, HyperNeRF reduces average error rates by 8.6% for novel-view synthesis as measured by LPIPS.
HyperNeRF represents the 5D radiance field corresponding to each individual input image as a slice through a higher-dimensional hyper-space, lifting NeRFs into a higher dimensional space.

Deformation-based NeRF approaches struggle to model changes in topology because topological changes require a discontinuity in the deformation field, but deformation fields are necessarily continuous.
HyperNeRF outperforms existing methods on both the smooth interpolation between scene moments task and the novel-view synthesis at fixed moments task.
The listed Hyper-NeRF (w/o deform) entry achieves a PSNR value of 27.4, SSIM of .895, and LPIPS of .253, with an additional value .0557 reported in the table row.
HyperNeRF's method outperforms all three baselines (Nerfies, Neural Volumes, NSFF) in most cases for the evaluated interpolation sequences.

fact_fields.method: comparative evaluation against Nerfies, Neural Volumes, NSFF

claim_records.text: HyperNeRF extends the domain of the template NeRF to a higher dimensional space (x, w) ∈ R^(3+W), where W is the number of higher dimensions, with the template NeRF represented as an MLP F: (x, w, d, ψ_i) → (c, σ).
HyperNeRF embeds the template NeRF in higher dimensions, where a slice taken by an intersecting high-dimensional slicing surface yields a full 3D NeRF.
HyperNeRF is evaluated on four datasets exhibiting topological changes: 3D Printer, Chicken, Expressions, and Peel Banana, with metrics computed on unseen validation views.
For view-synthesis, HyperNeRF compares against NeRF, Neural Volumes, NSFF, and Nerfies; for interpolation, it compares against NeRF, Nerfies, and Neural Volumes.
Neural Volumes is only evaluated on a central crop for interpolation error metrics because it works with fixed size inputs, resulting in slightly improved results for this baseline.
HyperNeRF's hyper-space template network is identical to the original NeRF MLP, except it takes an additional ambient coordinate and an appearance latent code ψ.
HyperNeRF's deformation network is identical to the deformation MLP of Nerfies.

HyperNeRF's ambient slicing surface network shares the input deformation code ω_i with the deformation network, uses a different windowed positional encoding parameter β, and directly outputs an ambient coordinate w.

fact_fields.method: HyperNeRF ambient slicing surface network architecture

claim_records.text: NeRF represents a scene as a continuous, volumetric field of density and radiance, defined as F: (x, d, ψ_i) → (c, σ), parameterized by an MLP that maps a 3D position x and viewing direction d to color c and density σ.
NeRF first maps each input x and d using a sinusoidal positional encoding γ(x) before providing coordinates to the MLP.
HyperNeRF is designed to accurately model the appearance and geometry of topologically varying scenes given a casually captured monocular image sequence.

claim_records.text: NeRF uses straight rays and fails to deal with complicated light path changes caused by refraction and reflection.
NeRF's limitation in handling refraction and reflection prevents it from successfully synthesizing transparent or specular objects.
The proposed refractive-reflective field takes object silhouette as input to reconstruct the geometry of non-Lambertian objects using marching tetrahedra with a progressive encoding.
The proposed refractive-reflective field models refraction and reflection effects of the object in a unified framework using Fresnel terms.
A virtual cone supersampling technique is proposed to achieve efficient and effective anti-aliasing.
The method is benchmarked on different shapes, backgrounds and Fresnel terms on both real-world and synthetic datasets.
Rendering results of various editing applications including material editing, object replacement/insertion, and environment illumination estimation are qualitatively and quantitatively benchmarked.

claim_records.text: Most current NeRF methods require intensive resources due to ray marching-based rendering.
Deformable Neural Mesh Primitive (DNMP) is designed to parameterize the entire urban scene for constructing urban-level radiance fields efficiently.

DNMP is a flexible and compact neural variant of classic mesh representation that enjoys both the efficiency of rasterization-based rendering and the powerful neural representation capability for photo-realistic image synthesis.
A DNMP consists of a set of connected deformable mesh vertices with paired vertex features to parameterize the geometry and radiance information of a local area.
The shape of each DNMP primitive is enforced to be decoded from a relatively low-dimensional latent space to constrain optimization degrees of freedom and lower storage budgets.
Rendering colors are decoded from vertex features (interpolated with rasterization) by a view-dependent MLP.
The DNMP method achieves leading performance for novel view synthesis in urban scenarios.
The DNMP representation enables fast rendering at 2.07ms per 1k pixels.
The DNMP representation has low peak memory usage of 110MB per 1k pixels.
The lightweight version of DNMP can run 33 times faster than vanilla NeRFs.
The lightweight version of DNMP has rendering speed of 0.61ms per 1k pixels, comparable to highly-optimized Instant-NGP's 0.71ms per 1k pixels.

claim_records.text: For IBRNet hierarchical volume sampling, both the coarse sample count Mc and fine sample count Mf are set to 64.
IBRNet's coarse sampling uses locations at equidistant disparity (inverse depth), resulting in equal intervals between adjacent point projections in pixel space.
IBRNet fine sampling uses an additional Mf locations informed by the coarse network prediction, and all Mc + Mf locations are used to render fine results.
IBRNet fine-tuned (Oursft) with 5 source views uses 0.04M parameters, 29M FLOPs per pixel, and achieves PSNR=25.80, SSIM=0.828, LPIPS=0.190.
IBRNet fine-tuned (Oursft) with 8 source views uses 45M FLOPs per pixel, and achieves PSNR=26.56, SSIM=0.847, LPIPS=0.176.
IBRNet fine-tuned (Oursft) with 10 source views uses 55M FLOPs per pixel, and achieves PSNR=26.73, SSIM=0.851, LPIPS=0.175.
NeRF uses 1.19M parameters, 304M FLOPs per pixel, and achieves PSNR=26.50, SSIM=0.811, LPIPS=0.250.
SRN uses 0.55M parameters, 5M FLOPs per pixel, and achieves PSNR=22.84, SSIM=0.668, LPIPS=0.378.
For IBRNet, the number of FLOPs scales roughly linearly with the number of source views.

IBRNet's pipeline consists of three parts: identifying nearby source views and extracting dense features, predicting volume densities and colors at continuous 5D locations, and using volume rendering to accumulate colors and densities along rays.
IBRNet can be trained end-to-end with an L2 loss on reconstructed image colors.
IBRNet's ray transformer module computes a scalar density value for each sample by considering density features along the entire ray, enabling visibility reasoning across larger spatial scales.
IBRNet's color blending module derives view-dependent color for each sample as a weighted combination of projected colors from source views.
IBRNet does not require precomputed geometry, discretized volume storage, or per-scene expensive training.

claims: The presented learning-based approach for representing dynamic objects is supervised directly from 2D images in a multi-view capture setting and does not require explicit reconstruction or tracking of the object.

The method has two primary components: an encoder-decoder network that transforms input images into a 3D volume representation, and a differentiable ray-marching operation that enables end-to-end training.
By virtue of its 3D representation, the construction extrapolates better to novel viewpoints compared to screen-space rendering techniques.
The encoder-decoder architecture learns a latent representation of a dynamic scene that enables production of novel content sequences not seen during training.

To overcome memory limitations of voxel-based representations, a dynamic irregular grid structure implemented with a warp field during ray-marching greatly improves apparent resolution and reduces grid-like artifacts and jagged motion.

Facial performance capture is used as a case in point to demonstrate incorporation of surface-based representations into the volumetric-learning framework for applications requiring the highest resolution.

An ablation experiment comparing direct voxel/warp estimation without an encoder-decoder network on four captured objects and one scene from a publicly available MVS dataset found that direct voxel/warp estimation contains artifacts and incorrectly reconstructs the object.
The inverse warp field W−1(x) maps output positions x to template sample locations y, and is defined as W−1(x) → y for x, y ∈ R3.

The inverse warp can represent details in the output space with higher resolution than uniform grid sampling, while remaining well-defined everywhere in the output space to provide usable gradients during learning.
The voxel grid decoder produces an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network, where g(z) produces a tensor of size 4×D×D×D for a D×D×D grid with 4 channel dimensions.
Textured meshes can efficiently and accurately represent fine detail in regions of the face like the skin and eyes while the voxel representation excels at modeling hair.

The system introduces a per-camera and per-channel gain д and bias b applied to the reconstructed image before comparing to ground truth to account for slight differences in overall image intensity across geometrically calibrated cameras.

Training the system consists of training the weights θ of the encoder-decoder network, alongside estimation of per-camera color calibration matrix and static background image, construction of the loss function, and use of reconstruction priors to improve accuracy.
The ray-marching discretization uses the rectangle rule twice with samples on the right of each step interval and backwards differences to discretize the derivative of α(t).

The encoder-decoder architecture learns a latent representation of a dynamic scene that enables real-time avatar driving based on user input, where the avatar's head turns to track the position of the user's hand.

Novel content generation via latent space interpolation produces intermediate frames reconstructed from linear interpolation between left and right real image encodings, with leftmost and rightmost frames reconstructed from real image encodings.
Conditioning the decoder on the head pose of the subject allows creation of novel sequences in real time.

claim_records.text: 3DGS-DET is the first work that introduces 3D Gaussian Splatting into indoor 3D Object Detection.
3DGS primarily relies on 2D pixel-level supervision, resulting in unclear 3D spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs and poor differentiation between objects and background, which hinders indoor 3DOD.
2D images typically include numerous background pixels, leading to densely reconstructed 3DGS with many noisy Gaussian blobs representing the background, negatively affecting detection.
Incorporating 2D Boundary Guidance significantly enhances the spatial distribution of Gaussian blobs, resulting in clearer differentiation between objects and their background.

The Box-Focused Sampling strategy uses 2D boxes to generate object probability distribution in 3D space, allowing effective probabilistic sampling in 3D to retain more object blobs and reduce noisy background blobs.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +6.0 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +7.8 on mAP@0.5 over NeRF-Det++ on the ScanNet dataset.
3DGS-DET achieves an improvement of +14.9 on mAP@0.25 over NeRF-Det++ on the ARKITScenes dataset.

claim_records.text: VDN-NeRF is a method for training neural radiance fields to obtain better geometry under non-Lambertian surface and dynamic lighting conditions that cause significant variation in the radiance of a point when viewed from different angles.

VDN-NeRF normalizes view-dependence by distilling invariant information already encoded in learned NeRFs, rather than explicitly modeling underlying factors that result in the view-dependent phenomenon.

VDN-NeRF applies to various baselines and significantly improves geometry without changing the volume rendering pipeline, even if the data is captured under a moving light source.

claim_records.text: Neural approaches such as NeRF have achieved remarkable success in view synthesis, but do not explicitly perform decomposition and instead operate exclusively on radiance, the product of reflectance and illumination.
Extensions to NeRF such as NeRD can perform decomposition but struggle to accurately recover detailed illumination, thereby significantly limiting realism.
The proposed reflectance decomposition network can estimate shape, BRDF, and per-image illumination given a set of object images captured under varying illumination.
Neural-PIL is a novel illumination integration network that replaces a costly illumination integral operation in the rendering with a simple network query.
Deep low-dimensional priors on BRDF and illumination representations are learned using novel smooth manifold auto-encoders.
The decompositions produced by the proposed method result in considerably better BRDF and light estimates, enabling more accurate novel view-synthesis and relighting compared to prior art.

fact_fields.method: proposed reflectance decomposition network with Neural-PIL

claim_records.text: NeuDA is a flexible neural implicit representation leveraging hierarchical voxel grids for high-fidelity surface reconstruction.
NeuDA maintains hierarchical anchor grids where each vertex stores a 3D position (anchor) instead of a direct embedding (feature).
NeuDA optimizes anchor grids such that different local geometry structures can be adaptively encoded.
NeuDA introduces a simple hierarchical positional encoding method for the hierarchical anchor structure to flexibly exploit properties of high-frequency and low-frequency geometry and appearance.
Experiments on both the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets demonstrate that NeuDA can produce promising mesh surfaces.
Previous works such as IDR and NeuS overlook spatial context in 3D space when predicting and rendering the surface, and may fail to capture sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures.

claim_records.text: In MVSNeRF, the neural feature f is trilinearly interpolated from the volume S at location x, where x is parameterized in the reference view's NDC space and d is represented by a unit vector at the reference view's coordinate.
Using NDC space in MVSNeRF effectively normalizes scene scales across different data sources, contributing to the method's good generalizability.
MVSNeRF applies positional encoding on position and direction vectors (x and d), which further enhances high-frequency details in results.
MVSNeRF is trained on the DTU dataset, partitioned into 88 training scenes and 16 testing scenes, using an image resolution of 512 × 640.
MVSNeRF uses f = 32 channels for feature extraction, which is also the number of feature channels in the cost volume and neural encoding volume before appending color channels.
MVSNeRF adopts D = 128 depth hypotheses uniformly sampled from near to far to specify the plane sweep volume.
MVSNeRF's MLP decoder consists of 6 layers, similar to NeRF's MLP but more compact.
For testing scenes, MVSNeRF selects 20 nearby views, uses 3 center views as input, 13 as additional input for per-scene fine-tuning, and the remaining 4 as testing views.
MVSNeRF models a neural radiance field that regresses volume density and view-dependent radiance in the scene from as few as three input images.
Once MVSNeRF's scene encoding volume S is reconstructed, this volume combined with the MLP decoder A can be used independently without the prepending 2D and 3D CNNs.

MVSNeRF enables applying differentiable volume rendering to regress image colors by reconstructing a neural encoding volume and regressing volume density and view-dependent radiance at arbitrary points in a scene.

MVSNeRF's pixel radiance value is computed by marching a ray through the pixel and accumulating radiance at sampled shading points on the ray, following the physically based volume rendering equation evaluated via differentiable ray marching.

fact_fields.method: MVSNeRF volume rendering via differentiable ray marching

claim_records.text: MVSNeRF's ray marching rendering is fully differentiable, allowing the framework to regress final pixel colors at novel viewpoints using three input views from end to end.
In MVSNeRF, given an arbitrary 3D location x and viewing direction d, an MLP A regresses the corresponding volume density σ and view-dependent radiance r from the neural encoding volume S.
MVSNeRF considers pixel colors c from the original images as additional input, concatenating colors from all views as a 3M-channel vector.
High-frequency details in MVSNeRF can be recovered in an augmented volume via a fast per-scene fine-tuning optimization.

claim_records.text: The 3D Gaussian Splatting method achieves high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis at 1080p resolution with display rates >= 30 fps.
The 3D Gaussian Splatting method represents scenes using 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse points produced during camera calibration.
The 3D Gaussian Splatting method performs interleaved optimization and density control of 3D Gaussians, including optimization of anisotropic covariance.
The 3D Gaussian Splatting method uses a fast visibility-aware rendering algorithm that supports anisotropic splatting.
The current state-of-the-art in image quality for novel-view synthesis prior to this work is Mip-NeRF360.
Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) introduced importance sampling and positional encoding to improve quality, but used a large Multi-Layer Perceptron that negatively affected speed.
The split densification strategy scales Gaussian volume by a factor of φ=1.6, determined experimentally.
An effective way to moderate the increase in the number of Gaussians is to set the α value close to zero every N=3000 iterations.
The 3D Gaussian Splatting method produces coarse, anisotropic Gaussians resulting in low-detail visuals as a failure artifact in background regions.
In views that have little overlap with those seen during training, the 3D Gaussian Splatting method may produce artifacts.
The 3D Gaussian Splatting method demonstrates that a continuous representation is not strictly necessary to allow fast and high-quality radiance field training.
Splitting big Gaussians is important to allow good reconstruction of the background.
Cloning small Gaussians instead of splitting them allows for a better and faster convergence especially when thin structures appear in the scene.
Initialization with SfM points helps reduce floaters compared to initialization with a random point cloud.

# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Field Optimized by Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents a static scene with one per-scene, fully connected, non-convolutional MLP over continuous 5D coordinates: 3D position and 2D viewing direction. Position determines volume density, while emitted RGB radiance may vary with viewing direction, allowing view-dependent effects without storing a mesh, voxel grid, or point cloud. Positional encoding lifts coordinates into sinusoidal features so the MLP can express high-frequency geometry and appearance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] Rendering casts a camera ray r(t) and integrates local radiance weighted by density and transmittance, C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, with T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds). NeRF approximates this integral at N samples: T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j) and the ray color is Σ_i(1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and photometric comparison are differentiable, posed RGB images update the network through the renderer. ## Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration or editing systems: first the scene representation, then the camera-ray volume-rendering operator, then the optimization setting and scope boundary. In the original formulation, a scene is represented by a fully connected, non-convolutional MLP that takes one continuous 5D coordinate—3D position plus 2D viewing direction—and returns volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location. The original paper groups its technical contribution around this 5D neural radiance field, differentiable classical volume rendering, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The learned object is therefore not an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. It is a continuous volumetric function queried at spatial locations along camera rays; density describes how strongly a point attenuates or emits light, while color or radiance may depend on the viewing direction, enabling non-Lambertian appearance such as specular effects. Later surveys describe the same core idea as generating color and density for points in the relevant 3D space rather than directly restoring an entire explicit geometry. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

For rendering, a camera ray is written parametrically as r(t), with direction d. The continuous color integral used in the NeRF family is C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds) is transmittance: the accumulated probability that light travels from the ray origin to depth t without being absorbed or stopped. In this formulation, σ is the density or absorption coefficient, c is the radiance sampled along the ray, and the integral composes local color contributions according to opacity and visibility. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

NeRF makes this integral tractable and differentiable by casting rays and evaluating the network at N discrete samples along each ray. A piecewise-constant approximation uses sample colors c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), densities σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)), and interval widths Δt_i; transmittance becomes T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and each sample contributes approximately (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because all operations—ray sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and image loss comparison—remain differentiable, RGB images with known camera poses provide gradients that update the MLP weights. This establishes the scope for the remaining sections: the foundational method explains per-scene novel-view synthesis, not the later efficiency, dynamic-scene, generative, or disentangled-material objectives that also use radiance-field ideas.
