## Background and Method Taxonomy

This taxonomy section uses a pipeline-centered grouping for the foundational NeRF problem: what the scene function stores, how a ray turns that field into a pixel, and how the renderer is optimized. It is an organizing choice for explaining the original method, not a universal taxonomy or a claim that later papers divide the field in exactly this way. The original NeRF paper itself names the linked components as a 5D neural radiance field, a differentiable volume-rendering procedure, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

At the representation level, the defining criterion is whether geometry and appearance are encoded as a continuous field queried by coordinates rather than as an explicit surface or discrete cache. Foundational NeRF maps a 3D position and a viewing direction to color and density through an MLP; later architectural work may replace or supplement that plain MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, tri-planes, voxel grids, or combinations. Those alternatives are related representations but often target different efficiency, memory, editing, or generalization trade-offs rather than changing the basic color-and-density answer supplied along a ray. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9]

At the rendering level, the relevant distinction is differentiable volumetric ray integration versus rasterization-oriented or baked representations. NeRF and closely following radiance-field methods cast camera rays, query density and radiance at sample positions, and composite those samples with transmittance. Explicit acceleration systems can precompute opacity, diffuse color, and features in sparse voxels or use mesh-like primitives and rasterization; these systems may preserve a NeRF-trained appearance model, but their execution path and cost structure are not the same as evaluating a large MLP hundreds of times per pixel during vanilla ray marching. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a]

At the optimization level, the foundational criterion is per-scene supervision from posed RGB images: rendered pixels are compared with observed images, and gradients propagate through the differentiable renderer into the network parameters. This differs from methods that introduce learned priors or generators to infer radiance fields from sparse or single-view input, and from methods that jointly estimate lighting and materials with physically based decomposition. Such methods can build on NeRF, but they add assumptions or latent variables beyond the original posed-image view-synthesis setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The temporal and scale axes should also be separated from the static foundational representation. Deformable-NeRF systems add a canonical field plus a deformation field, or use higher-dimensional ambient/latent coordinates, to model non-rigid or topologically changing observations; mip-oriented systems replace a point query with scale-aware frustum or multiscale-grid information to reduce aliasing. These are extensions of the coordinate-and-rendering framework, not ingredients required by the original static NeRF definition. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a]

Finally, the rendering equation should be distinguished from the numerical estimator used in training. Conceptually, NeRF relies on a continuous volume-rendering integral of view-dependent color weighted by density and transmittance; computationally, it approximates that integral with finite samples, interval widths, alpha values, and cumulative transmittance. Hierarchical sampling is an allocation strategy for those samples, while positional encoding is an input transformation that helps the MLP express high-frequency detail. Keeping field, integral, estimator, sampling, and encoding separate avoids conflating the foundational representation with later acceleration grids, sampling toolboxes, or real-time rendering back ends. ## Representative Methods

The foundational method is NeRF as introduced for novel view synthesis: one fully connected, non-convolutional network is optimized per scene from a sparse set of posed RGB images. Its input is a single continuous 5D coordinate consisting of the spatial location (x,y,z) and the viewing direction (θ,φ), and its output is the volume density at that location plus view-dependent emitted radiance or color. The network therefore defines a continuous volumetric scene function rather than storing a discrete mesh, voxel grid, or image-based surface model. This representation is intended for static scenes with known camera poses; the original claim is photorealistic synthesis of complicated geometry and appearance, not a general solution to dynamic scenes, camera estimation, or single-image generative reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] The two outputs play different roles in the physical model. Density σ is queried from position alone in the original architecture, so it describes occupancy-like or absorption-like scene structure at a 3D point independent of where the observer looks. Color c is an RGB radiance value and is allowed to depend on both the 3D point and the viewing direction. Conditioning color on direction is what lets the same learned field represent view-dependent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, while density remains the quantity used to accumulate visibility along a ray. The original paper reports this as emitted radiance; it is not, by itself, a disentangled model of surface albedo, roughness, incident illumination, or inter-reflection. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The MLP is not given raw coordinates only. NeRF applies a sinusoidal positional encoding γ to spatial coordinates and viewing directions, mapping each coordinate into sine and cosine features at increasing frequencies. In the notation used by later NeRF descriptions, γ(x) includes x and terms sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx) over frequency bands controlled by a hyperparameter. The purpose is to lift low-dimensional coordinates into a higher-dimensional space so the MLP can represent high-frequency geometry and appearance rather than being biased toward overly smooth functions. Positional encoding is thus an input transformation supporting expressivity; it is distinct from the density-color field itself and from the rendering operator. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

To turn the field into an image, NeRF traces one camera ray r through each pixel and writes points on that ray as r(t) with ray direction d. The continuous volume-rendering formulation used by the method is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds). T(t) is transmittance: the probability or fraction of light that reaches depth t along the ray without having been absorbed or stopped by earlier density. The integrand therefore says that a local color contributes in proportion both to the local opacity generated by density and to the visibility that the point has from the camera. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The continuous integral is not evaluated exactly. NeRF queries the network at N samples t̃_i along each ray and treats density and color as piecewise constant over the neighboring interval of width Δt_i. Writing σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)) and c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), the discrete transmittance is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and the rendered ray color is the sum Σ_i (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i)) c_i T_i. The term α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i) is the alpha or opacity assigned to the finite interval, while T_i is the product-like visibility inherited from all preceding samples. This alpha-compositing estimator is the computational form of classical volume rendering used in NeRF. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Differentiability comes from composing ordinary differentiable neural-network evaluations with the sampled ray integral. A rendered pixel color is a weighted sum of network outputs using α_i and T_i, and the rendered image is compared with the observed training image under a photometric loss. Gradients can therefore propagate from the pixel error through the compositing weights and sampled colors and densities into the MLP parameters. The original method states that posed images are the only input required for this optimization because the volume-rendering projection is naturally differentiable. Camera rays, sample positions, interval widths, and the known viewing directions are supplied by the camera model rather than learned by the basic pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

A practical contribution of the original method is hierarchical volume sampling. NeRF uses a coarse network and a fine network: the coarse pass samples points more broadly along the ray, produces a coarse rendering, and uses the resulting distribution to place additional samples in regions that are more likely to contain visible scene content. The fine pass then evaluates the fine network at the refined sample set. This is a capacity-allocation mechanism for the ray estimator; it does not change the definition of the 5D field or the transmittance-based color integral. Its role is to avoid spending the same number of MLP evaluations uniformly across empty space and occluded intervals. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The training objective follows the two-pass estimator. Both the coarse and fine rendered images are supervised against the corresponding ground-truth pixels; the original paper reports using a coarse-plus-fine photometric loss rather than optimizing only the final fine image. The coarse output is therefore not merely a proposal used without supervision: its error also supplies a learning signal for where density should be placed. After training, a novel view is rendered by casting rays from a new camera pose and evaluating the learned field along those rays. No 3D ground-truth density, surface mesh, or material labels are required in the foundational setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The mechanism also explains why NeRF can represent effects that challenge explicit surface reconstruction. Because color and density are distributed continuously in space and integrated along rays, the same formulation can synthesize thin structures, semi-transparent materials, occlusion, and view-dependent appearance without first requiring a tracked mesh or an explicit binary surface. Later deformable-NeRF work explicitly attributes this strength to NeRF's encoding of color and density by location and viewing angle, followed by volume rendering. This capability concerns image formation along rays; it does not imply that the learned density is always a unique or reliable geometric reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than the broader radiance-field literature. It optimizes a separate neural continuous volume representation for each scene from multiple posed views, and the original method does not provide a feed-forward model that generalizes across scenes, a generator for one-image reconstruction, a deformation model for moving objects, or a decomposition into lighting and materials. Later systems add priors, latent codes, deformation fields, hash or voxel encodings, multiscale frustum queries, or physically based incident-light fields. Those systems may reuse the color-density-and-ray-compositing idea, but they introduce additional assumptions and parameters beyond the original formulation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] In particular, later acceleration architectures should not be confused with the foundational representation. Vanilla NeRF evaluates a large MLP at many sample positions along every pixel ray; subsequent work bakes fields into sparse voxels, uses hash tables or hybrid feature grids, or introduces rasterization-oriented primitives to reduce training or rendering cost. These designs alter storage and computation and can change memory use and speed, but the core NeRF answer at a queried location remains conceptually a color or feature plus density that is integrated along a ray. The original method's contribution is the continuous 5D field and its differentiable volumetric optimization, whereas real-time performance is a separate engineering and representation objective. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] Taken together, the method has a tightly coupled chain: positional-encoded 5D coordinates are mapped by an MLP to density and view-dependent color; camera rays sample that continuous field; transmittance and interval opacity composite the samples into pixel colors; and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to fit the scene. The continuous integral supplies the conceptual volume-rendering model, while finite stratified and hierarchical samples make optimization and rendering tractable. This chain is the foundational NeRF mechanism on which later dynamic, accelerated, multiscale, generative, and inverse-rendering systems build. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

For the foundational NeRF question, the relevant experimental comparison is not a ranking against later accelerators: the original method is evaluated as a per-scene optimization system in which posed RGB images supervise a continuous 5D MLP through differentiable volume rendering. Its evidence chain has three linked parts: querying coordinates along camera rays, alpha-compositing density and color into rendered pixels, and comparing those pixels with training views to update the network. Later sources corroborate the same rendering computation, but their speed or memory numbers generally come from different architectures and therefore cannot be used to infer the original NeRF's runtime or quality under matched settings. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The task setting in the foundational paper is novel-view synthesis from a sparse set of input views with known camera poses. The learned representation is scene-specific: one fully connected network is fitted to the observations, rather than a feed-forward network being trained to reconstruct unseen scenes directly. The reported experimental claim in the paper is that this continuous volumetric scene function, optimized through classical volume rendering, outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis approaches and renders photorealistic novel views of complicated geometry and appearance. The selected source excerpts do not provide the exact benchmark tables, metric values, or training budgets, so those quantitative results should not be reconstructed here. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

The controlled variables in the method's own ablation logic are the components named by the paper: the 5D neural radiance field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling. Hierarchical sampling is evaluated as part of the same rendering pipeline by running coarse and fine networks along each ray and supervising their rendered colors; it changes where MLP evaluations are allocated along the ray, not the underlying color-and-density field. Positional encoding changes the network inputs so high-frequency variation can be expressed. Thus, comparisons that isolate these components should be interpreted as tests of the original per-scene pipeline, not as evidence that every later grid, hash-table, or rasterization method is equivalent. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

The rendering experiment is mathematically tied to the estimator described in the method. For a ray r(t), the continuous target color is an integral of view-dependent color c, density σ, and transmittance T; in the discrete implementation, N samples use σ_i, c_i, interval width Δt_i, T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and weights (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))T_i. A later exposition explicitly describes this as a discretized, differentiable volume ray-casting algorithm and notes that it assumes the fields are piecewise constant around samples. Consequently, image error can be back-propagated into sample colors and densities without requiring a separately differentiable surface rasterizer. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

Comparable settings matter when placing NeRF beside later efficient representations. Vanilla NeRF's characteristic cost is that a large MLP is evaluated at hundreds of sample positions along each pixel ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; this is why the original rendering process is described as too slow for interactive visualization. That statement identifies the computational mechanism, but it is not by itself a matched benchmark result. Sparse-voxel baking, multiresolution hash encodings, hybrid grids, Gaussian splatting, mesh primitives, or sampling toolboxes alter the data structure, number of network evaluations, parallelism, or rendering path, so their reported frame rates, memory use, and training times are not directly interchangeable with foundational NeRF unless the same scenes, resolutions, hardware, sample counts, and optimization schedules are reported. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

The selected acceleration literature illustrates these non-comparable conditions rather than supplying a single fair ranking. SNeRG bakes NeRF into a sparse 3D voxel grid whose active voxels store opacity, diffuse color, and a learned feature vector, then accumulates precomputed quantities by ray marching and uses a lightweight MLP for a view-dependent residual; the source states that this deferred approach increases rendering speed by three orders of magnitude but also requires substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF is introduced to run on common devices, while Hyb-NeRF combines learnable positional features at coarse levels with hash-based feature grids at fine levels and reports faster rendering, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint than the previous methods it evaluated. These are architecture-specific outcomes, not measurements of the original MLP-only formulation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

Other reported efficiency numbers are even less comparable because they target different scene scales and back ends. DNMP parameterizes urban scenes with deformable neural mesh primitives and reports 2.07 ms per 1,000 pixels, 110 MB peak memory per 1,000 pixels, a lightweight version 33 times faster than vanilla NeRF, and 0.61 versus 0.71 ms per 1,000 pixels relative to highly optimized Instant-NGP. UE4-NeRF instead partitions large scenes into sub-NeRFs, uses optimized polygonal meshes and levels of detail inside Unreal Engine 4, and reports up to 43 FPS at 4K. These systems use rasterization-oriented or mesh-assisted execution; they do not measure the same estimator as an MLP evaluated through hundreds of volumetric samples per pixel. [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:21e7ff8d96cd]

Sampling acceleration also needs to be separated from representation replacement. NerfAcc studies sampling methods under a unified transmittance-estimator concept and reports 1.5× to 20× training-time reductions across several recent NeRF variants with minimal code changes, including a native PyTorch implementation of highly customized Instant-NGP-style methods. That range reflects multiple methods and implementations rather than one fixed multiplier for foundational NeRF. It supports the conclusion that sample allocation and proposal/estimation strategies are major experimental axes in NeRF systems, but it does not show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy is obsolete or that quality is preserved under every setting. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Extensions evaluated on dynamic, scale-aware, generative, or inverse-rendering tasks should likewise not be pooled into the foundational novel-view-synthesis benchmark. Nerfies adds a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation field for casual non-rigid capture; HyperNeRF lifts the field into a higher-dimensional space for topology-varying scenes and reports LPIPS average-error reductions of 4.1% for interpolation and 8.6% for novel-view synthesis relative to Nerfies; Mip-VoG targets multiscale anti-aliased real-time rendering; NeILF jointly estimates geometry, materials, and lighting; and single-view or diffusion-based methods add learned priors absent from the original setup. Their datasets, supervision, outputs, and failure modes differ, so their metrics do not rank the static posed-image NeRF formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The experimentally defensible summary is therefore narrow: foundational NeRF demonstrates that a continuous coordinate-to-density-and-color MLP can be optimized per scene through a sampled, differentiable volume-rendering loss from posed RGB images, with hierarchical sampling and positional encoding as core design components. The evidence supports photorealistic novel-view synthesis and the ability to model view-dependent and volumetric appearance, while later papers establish that changing the representation and rendering path can substantially improve training or rendering efficiency. Because the selected excerpts do not contain a unified benchmark with identical datasets, hardware, resolution, sample counts, and metrics for all these systems, no cross-architecture numerical ranking can be inferred. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The central open limitation follows directly from the foundational estimator: NeRF does not evaluate a closed-form surface integral, but queries an MLP at many discrete positions along every camera ray and approximates the continuous transmittance-weighted color integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance, and identify this ray-marching workload as the reason rendering is far too slow for interactive visualization. The implication is not merely inconvenient runtime: training and inference both repeat dense neural evaluations over empty, occupied, and occluded intervals, so high visual fidelity is coupled in the original design to substantial per-pixel computation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] This cost has two distinct dimensions that should not be collapsed. Training is slow because rendered views must be generated and differentiated through many network queries before photometric gradients update the field; rendering is slow because novel pixels require the same sample-and-integrate process. Work on sampling toolboxes reports that optimizing and rendering NeRFs is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering, and that improved transmittance-estimation or sampling strategies can reduce training time across NeRF variants. Those results treat sample allocation as a systems and estimator problem, but they also show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy does not remove the underlying many-sample requirement. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

The usual acceleration response introduces a representation trade-off rather than a free improvement. Baking a NeRF into a sparse voxel grid can make rendering much faster, but SNeRG-style caching stores opacity, diffuse color, and learned features in volumetric textures; the selected MobileNeRF discussion states that this approach still ray marches through a sparse grid, cannot fully exploit commodity GPU parallelism, and needs significant GPU memory, which prevents execution on common mobile devices. Thus, replacing MLP evaluations with explicit caches may shift cost from network computation to storage, texture access, and memory bandwidth rather than eliminating resource demand. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] Hybrid encodings expose the same trade-off from another direction. Hash tables and feature grids can converge and render faster than a plain MLP because much of the scene signal is stored in shallow, local data structures, but surveys and distillation work note that these representations have less clear geometric meaning and can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing. Conversely, purely implicit MLP representations are described as comparatively convenient for some texture, lighting, deformation, stylization, and dynamic-modeling operations, while explicit or hybrid structures often train faster and support geometry-aware manipulation more directly. The open problem is therefore task-dependent deployment: compactness, editability, geometric interpretability, optimization speed, and rendering speed do not reduce to one universally dominant architecture. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:291b93a733e7]

A second foundational limitation is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only requires a field's accumulated colors and densities along rays to explain the training images; it does not require density to coincide with a unique, clean surface. Later geometry-oriented work states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable when view-dependent effects and changing lighting can be absorbed by the radiance field, and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce that effect on geometry. Consequently, a NeRF can produce convincing novel views while leaving occupancy, surface location, or the division between geometry and appearance underdetermined from the selected viewpoint and image loss alone. [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] The view-dependent color channel is both a capability and a source of this ambiguity. Letting color depend on viewing direction enables non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, but the original emitted-radiance output does not separately identify albedo, roughness, incident illumination, shadows, or inter-reflection. Methods such as NeILF add a neural incident light field and physically based inter-reflection constraints precisely to jointly estimate geometry, materials, and lighting. The need for those extra fields and constraints indicates that the foundational color-and-density representation is optimized for view synthesis, not by itself for a uniquely decomposed inverse-rendering solution. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

The discretized volume model also has approximation limits. The differentiable ray-casting exposition cited here makes the piecewise-constant assumption explicit: density and color are treated as constant around each sampled neighborhood when the continuous integral is replaced by finite alpha weights. If samples are too sparse, or the sampling distribution misses thin or high-frequency structure, the estimator can misestimate opacity and color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this by biasing later samples toward regions with visible content, but it is a heuristic allocation strategy dependent on the coarse pass; it is not an exact quadrature rule or a guarantee that all relevant geometry is sampled. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Scale and aliasing create a separate failure mode. The original point query takes a single 3D coordinate and viewing direction, so it does not explicitly encode the conical footprint or scale of a camera pixel. Mip-VoG states that NeRF yields blurred results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales and aliasing artifacts for distant test views, while Mip-NeRF addresses scale with a conical-frustum representation but remains offline because integrated positional encoding still requires MLP queries. This shows that high quality under one sampling scale does not automatically imply consistent anti-aliased rendering across resolutions or camera distances. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Static NeRF also does not solve non-rigid or topology-changing scenes. The foundational field is a static coordinate-to-color-and-density function fitted per scene. Nerfies extends it with a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation fields conditioned on latent codes for casually captured deformable scenes; HyperNeRF further argues that continuous deformation-based approaches struggle when topology changes, because a discontinuity in correspondence conflicts with a continuous deformation field, and instead lifts the radiance field into a higher-dimensional space. These extensions demonstrate that motion, changing topology, and temporal correspondence are additional assumptions outside the original static volume-rendering formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] Finally, per-scene optimization and known posed images limit the original applicability. The basic pipeline needs multiple views with camera poses and optimizes a separate network for each scene; it is not a feed-forward reconstruction model for arbitrary unseen scenes or a single-image generative model. Single-view and diffusion-based systems add learned priors or generators to fill unobserved content, while generative approaches such as Pix2NeRF may additionally be restricted to one object category per dataset. These limitations should be stated as boundaries of the foundational NeRF evidence: the differentiable renderer explains how posed multi-view images supervise a radiance field, but it does not itself supply camera localization, cross-scene generalization, priors for unseen regions, or real-time performance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471]

## Conclusion

The central answer is that NeRF is a continuous coordinate-based radiance-and-density field, not an explicit geometric cache, and its image-formation model is transmittance-weighted volume rendering along camera rays. The discrete alpha-compositing estimator makes the classical rendering integral tractable and differentiable, so multi-view RGB error can train density and color jointly without 3D labels. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The main trade-off in the foundational design is expressiveness against computation and geometric specificity. Continuous density and view-dependent color can represent occlusion, thin or semi-transparent structure, and specular appearance, but vanilla training and rendering require many MLP evaluations along rays, and convincing images do not guarantee a unique surface or a decomposition into albedo, roughness, and illumination. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] Hierarchical sampling and positional encoding are supporting components rather than replacements for the core representation: one refines where samples are placed, and the other improves high-frequency expressivity. Later grids, hash encodings, baking, rasterization, deformation, anti-aliasing, generative, and inverse-rendering methods extend or alter this pipeline under additional assumptions; their efficiency or task results should not be treated as matched measurements of original NeRF. # Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Field Optimized by Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents a static scene with one per-scene, fully connected, non-convolutional MLP over continuous 5D coordinates: 3D position and 2D viewing direction. Position determines volume density, while emitted RGB radiance may vary with viewing direction, allowing view-dependent effects without storing a mesh, voxel grid, or point cloud. Positional encoding lifts coordinates into sinusoidal features so the MLP can express high-frequency geometry and appearance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] Rendering casts a camera ray r(t) and integrates local radiance weighted by density and transmittance, C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, with T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds). NeRF approximates this integral at N samples: T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j) and the ray color is Σ_i(1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and photometric comparison are differentiable, posed RGB images update the network through the renderer. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more network evaluations to intervals likely to contain visible content, while both coarse and fine outputs receive photometric supervision in the original setup. The formulation supports per-scene novel-view synthesis of volumetric and view-dependent appearance, but it is not, by itself, a feed-forward reconstructor, dynamic-scene model, material-and-lighting decomposition, or real-time rendering system. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a]

## Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration or editing systems: first the scene representation, then the camera-ray volume-rendering operator, then the optimization setting and scope boundary. In the original formulation, a scene is represented by a fully connected, non-convolutional MLP that takes one continuous 5D coordinate—3D position plus 2D viewing direction—and returns volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location. The original paper groups its technical contribution around this 5D neural radiance field, differentiable classical volume rendering, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The learned object is therefore not an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. It is a continuous volumetric function queried at spatial locations along camera rays; density describes how strongly a point attenuates or emits light, while color or radiance may depend on the viewing direction, enabling non-Lambertian appearance such as specular effects. Later surveys describe the same core idea as generating color and density for points in the relevant 3D space rather than directly restoring an entire explicit geometry. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

For rendering, a camera ray is written parametrically as r(t), with direction d. The continuous color integral used in the NeRF family is C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds) is transmittance: the accumulated probability that light travels from the ray origin to depth t without being absorbed or stopped. In this formulation, σ is the density or absorption coefficient, c is the radiance sampled along the ray, and the integral composes local color contributions according to opacity and visibility. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

NeRF makes this integral tractable and differentiable by casting rays and evaluating the network at N discrete samples along each ray. A piecewise-constant approximation uses sample colors c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), densities σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)), and interval widths Δt_i; transmittance becomes T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and each sample contributes approximately (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because all operations—ray sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and image loss comparison—remain differentiable, RGB images with known camera poses provide gradients that update the MLP weights. This establishes the scope for the remaining sections: the foundational method explains per-scene novel-view synthesis, not the later efficiency, dynamic-scene, generative, or disentangled-material objectives that also use radiance-field ideas. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

This taxonomy section uses a pipeline-centered grouping for the foundational NeRF problem: what the scene function stores, how a ray turns that field into a pixel, and how the renderer is optimized. It is an organizing choice for explaining the original method, not a universal taxonomy or a claim that later papers divide the field in exactly this way. The original NeRF paper itself names the linked components as a 5D neural radiance field, a differentiable volume-rendering procedure, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

At the representation level, the defining criterion is whether geometry and appearance are encoded as a continuous field queried by coordinates rather than as an explicit surface or discrete cache. Foundational NeRF maps a 3D position and a viewing direction to color and density through an MLP; later architectural work may replace or supplement that plain MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, tri-planes, voxel grids, or combinations. Those alternatives are related representations but often target different efficiency, memory, editing, or generalization trade-offs rather than changing the basic color-and-density answer supplied along a ray. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9]

At the rendering level, the relevant distinction is differentiable volumetric ray integration versus rasterization-oriented or baked representations. NeRF and closely following radiance-field methods cast camera rays, query density and radiance at sample positions, and composite those samples with transmittance. Explicit acceleration systems can precompute opacity, diffuse color, and features in sparse voxels or use mesh-like primitives and rasterization; these systems may preserve a NeRF-trained appearance model, but their execution path and cost structure are not the same as evaluating a large MLP hundreds of times per pixel during vanilla ray marching. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a]

At the optimization level, the foundational criterion is per-scene supervision from posed RGB images: rendered pixels are compared with observed images, and gradients propagate through the differentiable renderer into the network parameters. This differs from methods that introduce learned priors or generators to infer radiance fields from sparse or single-view input, and from methods that jointly estimate lighting and materials with physically based decomposition. Such methods can build on NeRF, but they add assumptions or latent variables beyond the original posed-image view-synthesis setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The temporal and scale axes should also be separated from the static foundational representation. Deformable-NeRF systems add a canonical field plus a deformation field, or use higher-dimensional ambient/latent coordinates, to model non-rigid or topologically changing observations; mip-oriented systems replace a point query with scale-aware frustum or multiscale-grid information to reduce aliasing. These are extensions of the coordinate-and-rendering framework, not ingredients required by the original static NeRF definition. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a]

Finally, the rendering equation should be distinguished from the numerical estimator used in training. Conceptually, NeRF relies on a continuous volume-rendering integral of view-dependent color weighted by density and transmittance; computationally, it approximates that integral with finite samples, interval widths, alpha values, and cumulative transmittance. Hierarchical sampling is an allocation strategy for those samples, while positional encoding is an input transformation that helps the MLP express high-frequency detail. Keeping field, integral, estimator, sampling, and encoding separate avoids conflating the foundational representation with later acceleration grids, sampling toolboxes, or real-time rendering back ends. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

## Representative Methods

The foundational method is NeRF as introduced for novel view synthesis: one fully connected, non-convolutional network is optimized per scene from a sparse set of posed RGB images. Its input is a single continuous 5D coordinate consisting of the spatial location (x,y,z) and the viewing direction (θ,φ), and its output is the volume density at that location plus view-dependent emitted radiance or color. The network therefore defines a continuous volumetric scene function rather than storing a discrete mesh, voxel grid, or image-based surface model. This representation is intended for static scenes with known camera poses; the original claim is photorealistic synthesis of complicated geometry and appearance, not a general solution to dynamic scenes, camera estimation, or single-image generative reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] The two outputs play different roles in the physical model. Density σ is queried from position alone in the original architecture, so it describes occupancy-like or absorption-like scene structure at a 3D point independent of where the observer looks. Color c is an RGB radiance value and is allowed to depend on both the 3D point and the viewing direction. Conditioning color on direction is what lets the same learned field represent view-dependent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, while density remains the quantity used to accumulate visibility along a ray. The original paper reports this as emitted radiance; it is not, by itself, a disentangled model of surface albedo, roughness, incident illumination, or inter-reflection. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The MLP is not given raw coordinates only. NeRF applies a sinusoidal positional encoding γ to spatial coordinates and viewing directions, mapping each coordinate into sine and cosine features at increasing frequencies. In the notation used by later NeRF descriptions, γ(x) includes x and terms sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx) over frequency bands controlled by a hyperparameter. The purpose is to lift low-dimensional coordinates into a higher-dimensional space so the MLP can represent high-frequency geometry and appearance rather than being biased toward overly smooth functions. Positional encoding is thus an input transformation supporting expressivity; it is distinct from the density-color field itself and from the rendering operator. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

To turn the field into an image, NeRF traces one camera ray r through each pixel and writes points on that ray as r(t) with ray direction d. The continuous volume-rendering formulation used by the method is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds). T(t) is transmittance: the probability or fraction of light that reaches depth t along the ray without having been absorbed or stopped by earlier density. The integrand therefore says that a local color contributes in proportion both to the local opacity generated by density and to the visibility that the point has from the camera. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The continuous integral is not evaluated exactly. NeRF queries the network at N samples t̃_i along each ray and treats density and color as piecewise constant over the neighboring interval of width Δt_i. Writing σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)) and c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), the discrete transmittance is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and the rendered ray color is the sum Σ_i (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i)) c_i T_i. The term α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i) is the alpha or opacity assigned to the finite interval, while T_i is the product-like visibility inherited from all preceding samples. This alpha-compositing estimator is the computational form of classical volume rendering used in NeRF. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Differentiability comes from composing ordinary differentiable neural-network evaluations with the sampled ray integral. A rendered pixel color is a weighted sum of network outputs using α_i and T_i, and the rendered image is compared with the observed training image under a photometric loss. Gradients can therefore propagate from the pixel error through the compositing weights and sampled colors and densities into the MLP parameters. The original method states that posed images are the only input required for this optimization because the volume-rendering projection is naturally differentiable. Camera rays, sample positions, interval widths, and the known viewing directions are supplied by the camera model rather than learned by the basic pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

A practical contribution of the original method is hierarchical volume sampling. NeRF uses a coarse network and a fine network: the coarse pass samples points more broadly along the ray, produces a coarse rendering, and uses the resulting distribution to place additional samples in regions that are more likely to contain visible scene content. The fine pass then evaluates the fine network at the refined sample set. This is a capacity-allocation mechanism for the ray estimator; it does not change the definition of the 5D field or the transmittance-based color integral. Its role is to avoid spending the same number of MLP evaluations uniformly across empty space and occluded intervals. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The training objective follows the two-pass estimator. Both the coarse and fine rendered images are supervised against the corresponding ground-truth pixels; the original paper reports using a coarse-plus-fine photometric loss rather than optimizing only the final fine image. The coarse output is therefore not merely a proposal used without supervision: its error also supplies a learning signal for where density should be placed. After training, a novel view is rendered by casting rays from a new camera pose and evaluating the learned field along those rays. No 3D ground-truth density, surface mesh, or material labels are required in the foundational setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The mechanism also explains why NeRF can represent effects that challenge explicit surface reconstruction. Because color and density are distributed continuously in space and integrated along rays, the same formulation can synthesize thin structures, semi-transparent materials, occlusion, and view-dependent appearance without first requiring a tracked mesh or an explicit binary surface. Later deformable-NeRF work explicitly attributes this strength to NeRF's encoding of color and density by location and viewing angle, followed by volume rendering. This capability concerns image formation along rays; it does not imply that the learned density is always a unique or reliable geometric reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than the broader radiance-field literature. It optimizes a separate neural continuous volume representation for each scene from multiple posed views, and the original method does not provide a feed-forward model that generalizes across scenes, a generator for one-image reconstruction, a deformation model for moving objects, or a decomposition into lighting and materials. Later systems add priors, latent codes, deformation fields, hash or voxel encodings, multiscale frustum queries, or physically based incident-light fields. Those systems may reuse the color-density-and-ray-compositing idea, but they introduce additional assumptions and parameters beyond the original formulation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] In particular, later acceleration architectures should not be confused with the foundational representation. Vanilla NeRF evaluates a large MLP at many sample positions along every pixel ray; subsequent work bakes fields into sparse voxels, uses hash tables or hybrid feature grids, or introduces rasterization-oriented primitives to reduce training or rendering cost. These designs alter storage and computation and can change memory use and speed, but the core NeRF answer at a queried location remains conceptually a color or feature plus density that is integrated along a ray. The original method's contribution is the continuous 5D field and its differentiable volumetric optimization, whereas real-time performance is a separate engineering and representation objective. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] Taken together, the method has a tightly coupled chain: positional-encoded 5D coordinates are mapped by an MLP to density and view-dependent color; camera rays sample that continuous field; transmittance and interval opacity composite the samples into pixel colors; and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to fit the scene. The continuous integral supplies the conceptual volume-rendering model, while finite stratified and hierarchical samples make optimization and rendering tractable. This chain is the foundational NeRF mechanism on which later dynamic, accelerated, multiscale, generative, and inverse-rendering systems build. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

For the foundational NeRF question, the relevant experimental comparison is not a ranking against later accelerators: the original method is evaluated as a per-scene optimization system in which posed RGB images supervise a continuous 5D MLP through differentiable volume rendering. Its evidence chain has three linked parts: querying coordinates along camera rays, alpha-compositing density and color into rendered pixels, and comparing those pixels with training views to update the network. Later sources corroborate the same rendering computation, but their speed or memory numbers generally come from different architectures and therefore cannot be used to infer the original NeRF's runtime or quality under matched settings. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The task setting in the foundational paper is novel-view synthesis from a sparse set of input views with known camera poses. The learned representation is scene-specific: one fully connected network is fitted to the observations, rather than a feed-forward network being trained to reconstruct unseen scenes directly. The reported experimental claim in the paper is that this continuous volumetric scene function, optimized through classical volume rendering, outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis approaches and renders photorealistic novel views of complicated geometry and appearance. The selected source excerpts do not provide the exact benchmark tables, metric values, or training budgets, so those quantitative results should not be reconstructed here. The controlled variables in the method's own ablation logic are the components named by the paper: the 5D neural radiance field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling. Hierarchical sampling is evaluated as part of the same rendering pipeline by running coarse and fine networks along each ray and supervising their rendered colors; it changes where MLP evaluations are allocated along the ray, not the underlying color-and-density field. Positional encoding changes the network inputs so high-frequency variation can be expressed. Thus, comparisons that isolate these components should be interpreted as tests of the original per-scene pipeline, not as evidence that every later grid, hash-table, or rasterization method is equivalent. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

The rendering experiment is mathematically tied to the estimator described in the method. For a ray r(t), the continuous target color is an integral of view-dependent color c, density σ, and transmittance T; in the discrete implementation, N samples use σ_i, c_i, interval width Δt_i, T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and weights (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))T_i. A later exposition explicitly describes this as a discretized, differentiable volume ray-casting algorithm and notes that it assumes the fields are piecewise constant around samples. Consequently, image error can be back-propagated into sample colors and densities without requiring a separately differentiable surface rasterizer. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

Comparable settings matter when placing NeRF beside later efficient representations. Vanilla NeRF's characteristic cost is that a large MLP is evaluated at hundreds of sample positions along each pixel ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; this is why the original rendering process is described as too slow for interactive visualization. That statement identifies the computational mechanism, but it is not by itself a matched benchmark result. Sparse-voxel baking, multiresolution hash encodings, hybrid grids, Gaussian splatting, mesh primitives, or sampling toolboxes alter the data structure, number of network evaluations, parallelism, or rendering path, so their reported frame rates, memory use, and training times are not directly interchangeable with foundational NeRF unless the same scenes, resolutions, hardware, sample counts, and optimization schedules are reported. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

The selected acceleration literature illustrates these non-comparable conditions rather than supplying a single fair ranking. SNeRG bakes NeRF into a sparse 3D voxel grid whose active voxels store opacity, diffuse color, and a learned feature vector, then accumulates precomputed quantities by ray marching and uses a lightweight MLP for a view-dependent residual; the source states that this deferred approach increases rendering speed by three orders of magnitude but also requires substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF is introduced to run on common devices, while Hyb-NeRF combines learnable positional features at coarse levels with hash-based feature grids at fine levels and reports faster rendering, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint than the previous methods it evaluated. These are architecture-specific outcomes, not measurements of the original MLP-only formulation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

Other reported efficiency numbers are even less comparable because they target different scene scales and back ends. DNMP parameterizes urban scenes with deformable neural mesh primitives and reports 2.07 ms per 1,000 pixels, 110 MB peak memory per 1,000 pixels, a lightweight version 33 times faster than vanilla NeRF, and 0.61 versus 0.71 ms per 1,000 pixels relative to highly optimized Instant-NGP. UE4-NeRF instead partitions large scenes into sub-NeRFs, uses optimized polygonal meshes and levels of detail inside Unreal Engine 4, and reports up to 43 FPS at 4K. These systems use rasterization-oriented or mesh-assisted execution; they do not measure the same estimator as an MLP evaluated through hundreds of volumetric samples per pixel. [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:21e7ff8d96cd]

Sampling acceleration also needs to be separated from representation replacement. NerfAcc studies sampling methods under a unified transmittance-estimator concept and reports 1.5× to 20× training-time reductions across several recent NeRF variants with minimal code changes, including a native PyTorch implementation of highly customized Instant-NGP-style methods. That range reflects multiple methods and implementations rather than one fixed multiplier for foundational NeRF. It supports the conclusion that sample allocation and proposal/estimation strategies are major experimental axes in NeRF systems, but it does not show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy is obsolete or that quality is preserved under every setting. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Extensions evaluated on dynamic, scale-aware, generative, or inverse-rendering tasks should likewise not be pooled into the foundational novel-view-synthesis benchmark. Nerfies adds a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation field for casual non-rigid capture; HyperNeRF lifts the field into a higher-dimensional space for topology-varying scenes and reports LPIPS average-error reductions of 4.1% for interpolation and 8.6% for novel-view synthesis relative to Nerfies; Mip-VoG targets multiscale anti-aliased real-time rendering; NeILF jointly estimates geometry, materials, and lighting; and single-view or diffusion-based methods add learned priors absent from the original setup. Their datasets, supervision, outputs, and failure modes differ, so their metrics do not rank the static posed-image NeRF formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The experimentally defensible summary is therefore narrow: foundational NeRF demonstrates that a continuous coordinate-to-density-and-color MLP can be optimized per scene through a sampled, differentiable volume-rendering loss from posed RGB images, with hierarchical sampling and positional encoding as core design components. The evidence supports photorealistic novel-view synthesis and the ability to model view-dependent and volumetric appearance, while later papers establish that changing the representation and rendering path can substantially improve training or rendering efficiency. Because the selected excerpts do not contain a unified benchmark with identical datasets, hardware, resolution, sample counts, and metrics for all these systems, no cross-architecture numerical ranking can be inferred. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The central open limitation follows directly from the foundational estimator: NeRF does not evaluate a closed-form surface integral, but queries an MLP at many discrete positions along every camera ray and approximates the continuous transmittance-weighted color integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance, and identify this ray-marching workload as the reason rendering is far too slow for interactive visualization. The implication is not merely inconvenient runtime: training and inference both repeat dense neural evaluations over empty, occupied, and occluded intervals, so high visual fidelity is coupled in the original design to substantial per-pixel computation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] This cost has two distinct dimensions that should not be collapsed. Training is slow because rendered views must be generated and differentiated through many network queries before photometric gradients update the field; rendering is slow because novel pixels require the same sample-and-integrate process. Work on sampling toolboxes reports that optimizing and rendering NeRFs is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering, and that improved transmittance-estimation or sampling strategies can reduce training time across NeRF variants. Those results treat sample allocation as a systems and estimator problem, but they also show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy does not remove the underlying many-sample requirement. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

The usual acceleration response introduces a representation trade-off rather than a free improvement. Baking a NeRF into a sparse voxel grid can make rendering much faster, but SNeRG-style caching stores opacity, diffuse color, and learned features in volumetric textures; the selected MobileNeRF discussion states that this approach still ray marches through a sparse grid, cannot fully exploit commodity GPU parallelism, and needs significant GPU memory, which prevents execution on common mobile devices. Thus, replacing MLP evaluations with explicit caches may shift cost from network computation to storage, texture access, and memory bandwidth rather than eliminating resource demand. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] Hybrid encodings expose the same trade-off from another direction. Hash tables and feature grids can converge and render faster than a plain MLP because much of the scene signal is stored in shallow, local data structures, but surveys and distillation work note that these representations have less clear geometric meaning and can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing. Conversely, purely implicit MLP representations are described as comparatively convenient for some texture, lighting, deformation, stylization, and dynamic-modeling operations, while explicit or hybrid structures often train faster and support geometry-aware manipulation more directly. The open problem is therefore task-dependent deployment: compactness, editability, geometric interpretability, optimization speed, and rendering speed do not reduce to one universally dominant architecture. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:291b93a733e7]

A second foundational limitation is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only requires a field's accumulated colors and densities along rays to explain the training images; it does not require density to coincide with a unique, clean surface. Later geometry-oriented work states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable when view-dependent effects and changing lighting can be absorbed by the radiance field, and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce that effect on geometry. Consequently, a NeRF can produce convincing novel views while leaving occupancy, surface location, or the division between geometry and appearance underdetermined from the selected viewpoint and image loss alone. [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] The view-dependent color channel is both a capability and a source of this ambiguity. Letting color depend on viewing direction enables non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, but the original emitted-radiance output does not separately identify albedo, roughness, incident illumination, shadows, or inter-reflection. Methods such as NeILF add a neural incident light field and physically based inter-reflection constraints precisely to jointly estimate geometry, materials, and lighting. The need for those extra fields and constraints indicates that the foundational color-and-density representation is optimized for view synthesis, not by itself for a uniquely decomposed inverse-rendering solution. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

The discretized volume model also has approximation limits. The differentiable ray-casting exposition cited here makes the piecewise-constant assumption explicit: density and color are treated as constant around each sampled neighborhood when the continuous integral is replaced by finite alpha weights. If samples are too sparse, or the sampling distribution misses thin or high-frequency structure, the estimator can misestimate opacity and color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this by biasing later samples toward regions with visible content, but it is a heuristic allocation strategy dependent on the coarse pass; it is not an exact quadrature rule or a guarantee that all relevant geometry is sampled. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Scale and aliasing create a separate failure mode. The original point query takes a single 3D coordinate and viewing direction, so it does not explicitly encode the conical footprint or scale of a camera pixel. Mip-VoG states that NeRF yields blurred results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales and aliasing artifacts for distant test views, while Mip-NeRF addresses scale with a conical-frustum representation but remains offline because integrated positional encoding still requires MLP queries. This shows that high quality under one sampling scale does not automatically imply consistent anti-aliased rendering across resolutions or camera distances. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Static NeRF also does not solve non-rigid or topology-changing scenes. The foundational field is a static coordinate-to-color-and-density function fitted per scene. Nerfies extends it with a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation fields conditioned on latent codes for casually captured deformable scenes; HyperNeRF further argues that continuous deformation-based approaches struggle when topology changes, because a discontinuity in correspondence conflicts with a continuous deformation field, and instead lifts the radiance field into a higher-dimensional space. These extensions demonstrate that motion, changing topology, and temporal correspondence are additional assumptions outside the original static volume-rendering formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] Finally, per-scene optimization and known posed images limit the original applicability. The basic pipeline needs multiple views with camera poses and optimizes a separate network for each scene; it is not a feed-forward reconstruction model for arbitrary unseen scenes or a single-image generative model. Single-view and diffusion-based systems add learned priors or generators to fill unobserved content, while generative approaches such as Pix2NeRF may additionally be restricted to one object category per dataset. These limitations should be stated as boundaries of the foundational NeRF evidence: the differentiable renderer explains how posed multi-view images supervise a radiance field, but it does not itself supply camera localization, cross-scene generalization, priors for unseen regions, or real-time performance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471]

## Conclusion

The central answer is that NeRF is a continuous coordinate-based radiance-and-density field, not an explicit geometric cache, and its image-formation model is transmittance-weighted volume rendering along camera rays. The discrete alpha-compositing estimator makes the classical rendering integral tractable and differentiable, so multi-view RGB error can train density and color jointly without 3D labels. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The main trade-off in the foundational design is expressiveness against computation and geometric specificity. Continuous density and view-dependent color can represent occlusion, thin or semi-transparent structure, and specular appearance, but vanilla training and rendering require many MLP evaluations along rays, and convincing images do not guarantee a unique surface or a decomposition into albedo, roughness, and illumination. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] Hierarchical sampling and positional encoding are supporting components rather than replacements for the core representation: one refines where samples are placed, and the other improves high-frequency expressivity. Later grids, hash encodings, baking, rasterization, deformation, anti-aliasing, generative, and inverse-rendering methods extend or alter this pipeline under additional assumptions; their efficiency or task results should not be treated as matched measurements of original NeRF. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]
