input.query: Explain the foundational NeRF representation and differentiable volume-rendering formulation.
input.survey:
# Foundational NeRF: A Continuous 5D Field Optimized by Differentiable Volume Rendering

## Abstract

Foundational NeRF represents a static scene with one per-scene, fully connected, non-convolutional MLP over continuous 5D coordinates: 3D position and 2D viewing direction. Position determines volume density, while emitted RGB radiance may vary with viewing direction, allowing view-dependent effects without storing a mesh, voxel grid, or point cloud. Positional encoding lifts coordinates into sinusoidal features so the MLP can express high-frequency geometry and appearance. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] Rendering casts a camera ray r(t) and integrates local radiance weighted by density and transmittance, C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, with T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds). NeRF approximates this integral at N samples: T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j) and the ray color is Σ_i(1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and photometric comparison are differentiable, posed RGB images update the network through the renderer. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling allocates more network evaluations to intervals likely to contain visible content, while both coarse and fine outputs receive photometric supervision in the original setup. The formulation supports per-scene novel-view synthesis of volumetric and view-dependent appearance, but it is not, by itself, a feed-forward reconstructor, dynamic-scene model, material-and-lighting decomposition, or real-time rendering system. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a]

## Introduction

This review is organized around the foundational NeRF pipeline rather than later acceleration or editing systems: first the scene representation, then the camera-ray volume-rendering operator, then the optimization setting and scope boundary. In the original formulation, a scene is represented by a fully connected, non-convolutional MLP that takes one continuous 5D coordinate—3D position plus 2D viewing direction—and returns volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that location. The original paper groups its technical contribution around this 5D neural radiance field, differentiable classical volume rendering, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The learned object is therefore not an explicit mesh, voxel array, or point cloud. It is a continuous volumetric function queried at spatial locations along camera rays; density describes how strongly a point attenuates or emits light, while color or radiance may depend on the viewing direction, enabling non-Lambertian appearance such as specular effects. Later surveys describe the same core idea as generating color and density for points in the relevant 3D space rather than directly restoring an entire explicit geometry. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

For rendering, a camera ray is written parametrically as r(t), with direction d. The continuous color integral used in the NeRF family is C(r)=∫c(r(t),d)σ(r(t))T(t)dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^tσ(r(s))ds) is transmittance: the accumulated probability that light travels from the ray origin to depth t without being absorbed or stopped. In this formulation, σ is the density or absorption coefficient, c is the radiance sampled along the ray, and the integral composes local color contributions according to opacity and visibility. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

NeRF makes this integral tractable and differentiable by casting rays and evaluating the network at N discrete samples along each ray. A piecewise-constant approximation uses sample colors c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), densities σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)), and interval widths Δt_i; transmittance becomes T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and each sample contributes approximately (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))c_iT_i. Because all operations—ray sampling, MLP evaluation, transmittance, alpha compositing, and image loss comparison—remain differentiable, RGB images with known camera poses provide gradients that update the MLP weights. This establishes the scope for the remaining sections: the foundational method explains per-scene novel-view synthesis, not the later efficiency, dynamic-scene, generative, or disentangled-material objectives that also use radiance-field ideas. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

This taxonomy section uses a pipeline-centered grouping for the foundational NeRF problem: what the scene function stores, how a ray turns that field into a pixel, and how the renderer is optimized. It is an organizing choice for explaining the original method, not a universal taxonomy or a claim that later papers divide the field in exactly this way. The original NeRF paper itself names the linked components as a 5D neural radiance field, a differentiable volume-rendering procedure, hierarchical sampling, and positional encoding. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

At the representation level, the defining criterion is whether geometry and appearance are encoded as a continuous field queried by coordinates rather than as an explicit surface or discrete cache. Foundational NeRF maps a 3D position and a viewing direction to color and density through an MLP; later architectural work may replace or supplement that plain MLP with sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables, tri-planes, voxel grids, or combinations. Those alternatives are related representations but often target different efficiency, memory, editing, or generalization trade-offs rather than changing the basic color-and-density answer supplied along a ray. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9]

At the rendering level, the relevant distinction is differentiable volumetric ray integration versus rasterization-oriented or baked representations. NeRF and closely following radiance-field methods cast camera rays, query density and radiance at sample positions, and composite those samples with transmittance. Explicit acceleration systems can precompute opacity, diffuse color, and features in sparse voxels or use mesh-like primitives and rasterization; these systems may preserve a NeRF-trained appearance model, but their execution path and cost structure are not the same as evaluating a large MLP hundreds of times per pixel during vanilla ray marching. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a]

At the optimization level, the foundational criterion is per-scene supervision from posed RGB images: rendered pixels are compared with observed images, and gradients propagate through the differentiable renderer into the network parameters. This differs from methods that introduce learned priors or generators to infer radiance fields from sparse or single-view input, and from methods that jointly estimate lighting and materials with physically based decomposition. Such methods can build on NeRF, but they add assumptions or latent variables beyond the original posed-image view-synthesis setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2302.10109:section:abstract:2:bae7bea14f6b:claim:de84373fd7ce] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The temporal and scale axes should also be separated from the static foundational representation. Deformable-NeRF systems add a canonical field plus a deformation field, or use higher-dimensional ambient/latent coordinates, to model non-rigid or topologically changing observations; mip-oriented systems replace a point query with scale-aware frustum or multiscale-grid information to reduce aliasing. These are extensions of the coordinate-and-rendering framework, not ingredients required by the original static NeRF definition. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a]

Finally, the rendering equation should be distinguished from the numerical estimator used in training. Conceptually, NeRF relies on a continuous volume-rendering integral of view-dependent color weighted by density and transmittance; computationally, it approximates that integral with finite samples, interval widths, alpha values, and cumulative transmittance. Hierarchical sampling is an allocation strategy for those samples, while positional encoding is an input transformation that helps the MLP express high-frequency detail. Keeping field, integral, estimator, sampling, and encoding separate avoids conflating the foundational representation with later acceleration grids, sampling toolboxes, or real-time rendering back ends. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

## Representative Methods

The foundational method is NeRF as introduced for novel view synthesis: one fully connected, non-convolutional network is optimized per scene from a sparse set of posed RGB images. Its input is a single continuous 5D coordinate consisting of the spatial location (x,y,z) and the viewing direction (θ,φ), and its output is the volume density at that location plus view-dependent emitted radiance or color. The network therefore defines a continuous volumetric scene function rather than storing a discrete mesh, voxel grid, or image-based surface model. This representation is intended for static scenes with known camera poses; the original claim is photorealistic synthesis of complicated geometry and appearance, not a general solution to dynamic scenes, camera estimation, or single-image generative reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] The two outputs play different roles in the physical model. Density σ is queried from position alone in the original architecture, so it describes occupancy-like or absorption-like scene structure at a 3D point independent of where the observer looks. Color c is an RGB radiance value and is allowed to depend on both the 3D point and the viewing direction. Conditioning color on direction is what lets the same learned field represent view-dependent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, while density remains the quantity used to accumulate visibility along a ray. The original paper reports this as emitted radiance; it is not, by itself, a disentangled model of surface albedo, roughness, incident illumination, or inter-reflection. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The MLP is not given raw coordinates only. NeRF applies a sinusoidal positional encoding γ to spatial coordinates and viewing directions, mapping each coordinate into sine and cosine features at increasing frequencies. In the notation used by later NeRF descriptions, γ(x) includes x and terms sin(2^kπx), cos(2^kπx) over frequency bands controlled by a hyperparameter. The purpose is to lift low-dimensional coordinates into a higher-dimensional space so the MLP can represent high-frequency geometry and appearance rather than being biased toward overly smooth functions. Positional encoding is thus an input transformation supporting expressivity; it is distinct from the density-color field itself and from the rendering operator. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

To turn the field into an image, NeRF traces one camera ray r through each pixel and writes points on that ray as r(t) with ray direction d. The continuous volume-rendering formulation used by the method is C(r)=∫ c(r(t),d) σ(r(t)) T(t) dt, where T(t)=exp(−∫_0^t σ(r(s))ds). T(t) is transmittance: the probability or fraction of light that reaches depth t along the ray without having been absorbed or stopped by earlier density. The integrand therefore says that a local color contributes in proportion both to the local opacity generated by density and to the visibility that the point has from the camera. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The continuous integral is not evaluated exactly. NeRF queries the network at N samples t̃_i along each ray and treats density and color as piecewise constant over the neighboring interval of width Δt_i. Writing σ_i=σ(r(t̃_i)) and c_i=c(r(t̃_i),d), the discrete transmittance is T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and the rendered ray color is the sum Σ_i (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i)) c_i T_i. The term α_i=1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i) is the alpha or opacity assigned to the finite interval, while T_i is the product-like visibility inherited from all preceding samples. This alpha-compositing estimator is the computational form of classical volume rendering used in NeRF. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Differentiability comes from composing ordinary differentiable neural-network evaluations with the sampled ray integral. A rendered pixel color is a weighted sum of network outputs using α_i and T_i, and the rendered image is compared with the observed training image under a photometric loss. Gradients can therefore propagate from the pixel error through the compositing weights and sampled colors and densities into the MLP parameters. The original method states that posed images are the only input required for this optimization because the volume-rendering projection is naturally differentiable. Camera rays, sample positions, interval widths, and the known viewing directions are supplied by the camera model rather than learned by the basic pipeline. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

A practical contribution of the original method is hierarchical volume sampling. NeRF uses a coarse network and a fine network: the coarse pass samples points more broadly along the ray, produces a coarse rendering, and uses the resulting distribution to place additional samples in regions that are more likely to contain visible scene content. The fine pass then evaluates the fine network at the refined sample set. This is a capacity-allocation mechanism for the ray estimator; it does not change the definition of the 5D field or the transmittance-based color integral. Its role is to avoid spending the same number of MLP evaluations uniformly across empty space and occluded intervals. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] The training objective follows the two-pass estimator. Both the coarse and fine rendered images are supervised against the corresponding ground-truth pixels; the original paper reports using a coarse-plus-fine photometric loss rather than optimizing only the final fine image. The coarse output is therefore not merely a proposal used without supervision: its error also supplies a learning signal for where density should be placed. After training, a novel view is rendered by casting rays from a new camera pose and evaluating the learned field along those rays. No 3D ground-truth density, surface mesh, or material labels are required in the foundational setup. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The mechanism also explains why NeRF can represent effects that challenge explicit surface reconstruction. Because color and density are distributed continuously in space and integrated along rays, the same formulation can synthesize thin structures, semi-transparent materials, occlusion, and view-dependent appearance without first requiring a tracked mesh or an explicit binary surface. Later deformable-NeRF work explicitly attributes this strength to NeRF's encoding of color and density by location and viewing angle, followed by volume rendering. This capability concerns image formation along rays; it does not imply that the learned density is always a unique or reliable geometric reconstruction. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The applicability boundary of foundational NeRF is narrower than the broader radiance-field literature. It optimizes a separate neural continuous volume representation for each scene from multiple posed views, and the original method does not provide a feed-forward model that generalizes across scenes, a generator for one-image reconstruction, a deformation model for moving objects, or a decomposition into lighting and materials. Later systems add priors, latent codes, deformation fields, hash or voxel encodings, multiscale frustum queries, or physically based incident-light fields. Those systems may reuse the color-density-and-ray-compositing idea, but they introduce additional assumptions and parameters beyond the original formulation. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:5_2_gan_based_approaches:0:b208ff0908a8:claim:75809321e471] [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] In particular, later acceleration architectures should not be confused with the foundational representation. Vanilla NeRF evaluates a large MLP at many sample positions along every pixel ray; subsequent work bakes fields into sparse voxels, uses hash tables or hybrid feature grids, or introduces rasterization-oriented primitives to reduce training or rendering cost. These designs alter storage and computation and can change memory use and speed, but the core NeRF answer at a queried location remains conceptually a color or feature plus density that is integrated along a ray. The original method's contribution is the continuous 5D field and its differentiable volumetric optimization, whereas real-time performance is a separate engineering and representation objective. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] Taken together, the method has a tightly coupled chain: positional-encoded 5D coordinates are mapped by an MLP to density and view-dependent color; camera rays sample that continuous field; transmittance and interval opacity composite the samples into pixel colors; and photometric error back-propagates through the renderer to fit the scene. The continuous integral supplies the conceptual volume-rendering model, while finite stratified and hierarchical samples make optimization and rendering tractable. This chain is the foundational NeRF mechanism on which later dynamic, accelerated, multiscale, generative, and inverse-rendering systems build. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

For the foundational NeRF question, the relevant experimental comparison is not a ranking against later accelerators: the original method is evaluated as a per-scene optimization system in which posed RGB images supervise a continuous 5D MLP through differentiable volume rendering. Its evidence chain has three linked parts: querying coordinates along camera rays, alpha-compositing density and color into rendered pixels, and comparing those pixels with training views to update the network. Later sources corroborate the same rendering computation, but their speed or memory numbers generally come from different architectures and therefore cannot be used to infer the original NeRF's runtime or quality under matched settings. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

The task setting in the foundational paper is novel-view synthesis from a sparse set of input views with known camera poses. The learned representation is scene-specific: one fully connected network is fitted to the observations, rather than a feed-forward network being trained to reconstruct unseen scenes directly. The reported experimental claim in the paper is that this continuous volumetric scene function, optimized through classical volume rendering, outperforms prior neural-rendering and view-synthesis approaches and renders photorealistic novel views of complicated geometry and appearance. The selected source excerpts do not provide the exact benchmark tables, metric values, or training budgets, so those quantitative results should not be reconstructed here. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

The controlled variables in the method's own ablation logic are the components named by the paper: the 5D neural radiance field, positional encoding, differentiable volume rendering, and hierarchical sampling. Hierarchical sampling is evaluated as part of the same rendering pipeline by running coarse and fine networks along each ray and supervising their rendered colors; it changes where MLP evaluations are allocated along the ray, not the underlying color-and-density field. Positional encoding changes the network inputs so high-frequency variation can be expressed. Thus, comparisons that isolate these components should be interpreted as tests of the original per-scene pipeline, not as evidence that every later grid, hash-table, or rasterization method is equivalent. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514]

The rendering experiment is mathematically tied to the estimator described in the method. For a ray r(t), the continuous target color is an integral of view-dependent color c, density σ, and transmittance T; in the discrete implementation, N samples use σ_i, c_i, interval width Δt_i, T_i=exp(−Σ_{j<i}σ_jΔt_j), and weights (1−exp(−σ_iΔt_i))T_i. A later exposition explicitly describes this as a discretized, differentiable volume ray-casting algorithm and notes that it assumes the fields are piecewise constant around samples. Consequently, image error can be back-propagated into sample colors and densities without requiring a separately differentiable surface rasterizer. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545]

Comparable settings matter when placing NeRF beside later efficient representations. Vanilla NeRF's characteristic cost is that a large MLP is evaluated at hundreds of sample positions along each pixel ray to estimate and integrate density and radiance; this is why the original rendering process is described as too slow for interactive visualization. That statement identifies the computational mechanism, but it is not by itself a matched benchmark result. Sparse-voxel baking, multiresolution hash encodings, hybrid grids, Gaussian splatting, mesh primitives, or sampling toolboxes alter the data structure, number of network evaluations, parallelism, or rendering path, so their reported frame rates, memory use, and training times are not directly interchangeable with foundational NeRF unless the same scenes, resolutions, hardware, sample counts, and optimization schedules are reported. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2308.04079:section:unknown:4:858f653b78f8:claim:9cb34a6ceb4a] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

The selected acceleration literature illustrates these non-comparable conditions rather than supplying a single fair ranking. SNeRG bakes NeRF into a sparse 3D voxel grid whose active voxels store opacity, diffuse color, and a learned feature vector, then accumulates precomputed quantities by ray marching and uses a lightweight MLP for a view-dependent residual; the source states that this deferred approach increases rendering speed by three orders of magnitude but also requires substantial GPU memory for volumetric textures. MobileNeRF is introduced to run on common devices, while Hyb-NeRF combines learnable positional features at coarse levels with hash-based feature grids at fine levels and reports faster rendering, better rendering quality, and lower memory footprint than the previous methods it evaluated. These are architecture-specific outcomes, not measurements of the original MLP-only formulation. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49]

Other reported efficiency numbers are even less comparable because they target different scene scales and back ends. DNMP parameterizes urban scenes with deformable neural mesh primitives and reports 2.07 ms per 1,000 pixels, 110 MB peak memory per 1,000 pixels, a lightweight version 33 times faster than vanilla NeRF, and 0.61 versus 0.71 ms per 1,000 pixels relative to highly optimized Instant-NGP. UE4-NeRF instead partitions large scenes into sub-NeRFs, uses optimized polygonal meshes and levels of detail inside Unreal Engine 4, and reports up to 43 FPS at 4K. These systems use rasterization-oriented or mesh-assisted execution; they do not measure the same estimator as an MLP evaluated through hundreds of volumetric samples per pixel. [E:arxiv:2307.10776:abstract:claim:d9d34a801f89] [E:arxiv:2310.13263:abstract:claim:21e7ff8d96cd]

Sampling acceleration also needs to be separated from representation replacement. NerfAcc studies sampling methods under a unified transmittance-estimator concept and reports 1.5× to 20× training-time reductions across several recent NeRF variants with minimal code changes, including a native PyTorch implementation of highly customized Instant-NGP-style methods. That range reflects multiple methods and implementations rather than one fixed multiplier for foundational NeRF. It supports the conclusion that sample allocation and proposal/estimation strategies are major experimental axes in NeRF systems, but it does not show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy is obsolete or that quality is preserved under every setting. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Extensions evaluated on dynamic, scale-aware, generative, or inverse-rendering tasks should likewise not be pooled into the foundational novel-view-synthesis benchmark. Nerfies adds a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation field for casual non-rigid capture; HyperNeRF lifts the field into a higher-dimensional space for topology-varying scenes and reports LPIPS average-error reductions of 4.1% for interpolation and 8.6% for novel-view synthesis relative to Nerfies; Mip-VoG targets multiscale anti-aliased real-time rendering; NeILF jointly estimates geometry, materials, and lighting; and single-view or diffusion-based methods add learned priors absent from the original setup. Their datasets, supervision, outputs, and failure modes differ, so their metrics do not rank the static posed-image NeRF formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d]

The experimentally defensible summary is therefore narrow: foundational NeRF demonstrates that a continuous coordinate-to-density-and-color MLP can be optimized per scene through a sampled, differentiable volume-rendering loss from posed RGB images, with hierarchical sampling and positional encoding as core design components. The evidence supports photorealistic novel-view synthesis and the ability to model view-dependent and volumetric appearance, while later papers establish that changing the representation and rendering path can substantially improve training or rendering efficiency. Because the selected excerpts do not contain a unified benchmark with identical datasets, hardware, resolution, sample counts, and metrics for all these systems, no cross-architecture numerical ranking can be inferred. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The central open limitation follows directly from the foundational estimator: NeRF does not evaluate a closed-form surface integral, but queries an MLP at many discrete positions along every camera ray and approximates the continuous transmittance-weighted color integral. Later efficiency papers describe vanilla NeRF as evaluating a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions per pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance, and identify this ray-marching workload as the reason rendering is far too slow for interactive visualization. The implication is not merely inconvenient runtime: training and inference both repeat dense neural evaluations over empty, occupied, and occluded intervals, so high visual fidelity is coupled in the original design to substantial per-pixel computation. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] This cost has two distinct dimensions that should not be collapsed. Training is slow because rendered views must be generated and differentiated through many network queries before photometric gradients update the field; rendering is slow because novel pixels require the same sample-and-integrate process. Work on sampling toolboxes reports that optimizing and rendering NeRFs is computationally expensive due to the vast number of samples required by volume rendering, and that improved transmittance-estimation or sampling strategies can reduce training time across NeRF variants. Those results treat sample allocation as a systems and estimator problem, but they also show that the original coarse-to-fine hierarchy does not remove the underlying many-sample requirement. [E:arxiv:2305.04966:abstract:claim:6a57fdaf85da] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb]

The usual acceleration response introduces a representation trade-off rather than a free improvement. Baking a NeRF into a sparse voxel grid can make rendering much faster, but SNeRG-style caching stores opacity, diffuse color, and learned features in volumetric textures; the selected MobileNeRF discussion states that this approach still ray marches through a sparse grid, cannot fully exploit commodity GPU parallelism, and needs significant GPU memory, which prevents execution on common mobile devices. Thus, replacing MLP evaluations with explicit caches may shift cost from network computation to storage, texture access, and memory bandwidth rather than eliminating resource demand. [E:arxiv:2208.00277:section:abstract:1:3cd62fc6d6ab:claim:1f0f40cc936b] [E:arxiv:2311.12490:abstract:claim:6c0aacb6ca49] Hybrid encodings expose the same trade-off from another direction. Hash tables and feature grids can converge and render faster than a plain MLP because much of the scene signal is stored in shallow, local data structures, but surveys and distillation work note that these representations have less clear geometric meaning and can hamper spatial-relation-aware editing. Conversely, purely implicit MLP representations are described as comparatively convenient for some texture, lighting, deformation, stylization, and dynamic-modeling operations, while explicit or hybrid structures often train faster and support geometry-aware manipulation more directly. The open problem is therefore task-dependent deployment: compactness, editability, geometric interpretability, optimization speed, and rendering speed do not reduce to one universally dominant architecture. [E:arxiv:2211.15977:abstract:claim:ed918e4d2514] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:f165d0a9495f] [E:arxiv:2211.15977:section:abstract:2:a55c10c0107f:claim:291b93a733e7]

A second foundational limitation is geometric ambiguity. The photometric renderer only requires a field's accumulated colors and densities along rays to explain the training images; it does not require density to coincide with a unique, clean surface. Later geometry-oriented work states that shape-radiance ambiguity is inevitable when view-dependent effects and changing lighting can be absorbed by the radiance field, and proposes view-dependence normalization to reduce that effect on geometry. Consequently, a NeRF can produce convincing novel views while leaving occupancy, surface location, or the division between geometry and appearance underdetermined from the selected viewpoint and image loss alone. [E:arxiv:2303.17968:abstract:claim:0acdecb8d9c0] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] The view-dependent color channel is both a capability and a source of this ambiguity. Letting color depend on viewing direction enables non-Lambertian effects such as specularities, but the original emitted-radiance output does not separately identify albedo, roughness, incident illumination, shadows, or inter-reflection. Methods such as NeILF add a neural incident light field and physically based inter-reflection constraints precisely to jointly estimate geometry, materials, and lighting. The need for those extra fields and constraints indicates that the foundational color-and-density representation is optimized for view synthesis, not by itself for a uniquely decomposed inverse-rendering solution. [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2303.17147:abstract:claim:b4248ee13c5d] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

The discretized volume model also has approximation limits. The differentiable ray-casting exposition cited here makes the piecewise-constant assumption explicit: density and color are treated as constant around each sampled neighborhood when the continuous integral is replaced by finite alpha weights. If samples are too sparse, or the sampling distribution misses thin or high-frequency structure, the estimator can misestimate opacity and color. Hierarchical sampling mitigates this by biasing later samples toward regions with visible content, but it is a heuristic allocation strategy dependent on the coarse pass; it is not an exact quadrature rule or a guarantee that all relevant geometry is sampled. [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] Scale and aliasing create a separate failure mode. The original point query takes a single 3D coordinate and viewing direction, so it does not explicitly encode the conical footprint or scale of a camera pixel. Mip-VoG states that NeRF yields blurred results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales and aliasing artifacts for distant test views, while Mip-NeRF addresses scale with a conical-frustum representation but remains offline because integrated positional encoding still requires MLP queries. This shows that high quality under one sampling scale does not automatically imply consistent anti-aliased rendering across resolutions or camera distances. [E:arxiv:2304.10075:abstract:claim:59db3c4bcf10] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564]

Static NeRF also does not solve non-rigid or topology-changing scenes. The foundational field is a static coordinate-to-color-and-density function fitted per scene. Nerfies extends it with a canonical NeRF and per-observation deformation fields conditioned on latent codes for casually captured deformable scenes; HyperNeRF further argues that continuous deformation-based approaches struggle when topology changes, because a discontinuity in correspondence conflicts with a continuous deformation field, and instead lifts the radiance field into a higher-dimensional space. These extensions demonstrate that motion, changing topology, and temporal correspondence are additional assumptions outside the original static volume-rendering formulation. [E:arxiv:2011.12948:section:abstract:3:260c2df009a6:claim:9fac2a545a62] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:section:unknown:29:ca4fb655fddc:claim:2fe10d42282a] [E:arxiv:2106.13228:abstract:claim:9d69903a79a6] Finally, per-scene optimization and known posed images limit the original applicability. The basic pipeline needs multiple views with camera poses and optimizes a separate network for each scene; it is not a feed-forward reconstruction model for arbitrary unseen scenes or a single-image generative model. Single-view and diffusion-based systems add learned priors or generators to fill unobserved content, while generative approaches such as Pix2NeRF may additionally be restricted to one object category per dataset. These limitations should be stated as boundaries of the foundational NeRF evidence: the differentiable renderer explains how posed multi-view images supervise a radiance field, but it does not itself supply camera localization, cross-scene generalization, priors for unseen regions, or real-time performance. ## Conclusion

The central answer is that NeRF is a continuous coordinate-based radiance-and-density field, not an explicit geometric cache, and its image-formation model is transmittance-weighted volume rendering along camera rays. The discrete alpha-compositing estimator makes the classical rendering integral tractable and differentiable, so multi-view RGB error can train density and color jointly without 3D labels. [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:5c83fd6dba94] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:abstract:claim:2a8e1f8afec9] [E:arxiv:2306.03000:section:unknown:2:26aa95755737:claim:cdb532ace514] [E:arxiv:2408.03356:section:abstract:4:1447cd6be2ee:claim:a8109ffcc2fb] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:abstract:claim:d706bf9b6545] [E:arxiv:2003.08934:section:unknown:6:45bbf170163b:claim:67e7dc5b0564] The main trade-off in the foundational design is expressiveness against computation and geometric specificity. Continuous density and view-dependent color can represent occlusion, thin or semi-transparent structure, and specular appearance, but vanilla training and rendering require many MLP evaluations along rays, and convincing images do not guarantee a unique surface or a decomposition into albedo, roughness, and illumination. claim_records.text: RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.
RayGauss achieves inference speeds of 25 FPS on the Blender dataset.

RayGauss provides a physically consistent formulation of emitted radiance c and density σ, decomposed with Gaussian functions associated with Spherical Gaussians/Harmonics for all-frequency colorimetric representation.
RayGauss introduces a method enabling differentiable ray casting of irregularly distributed Gaussians using an algorithm that integrates radiance fields slab by slab and leverages a BVH structure.
RayGauss achieves superior rendering quality compared to the state-of-the-art while maintaining reasonable training times.

RayGauss proposes a novel definition of radiance fields based on their decomposition into a weighted sum of locally supported elliptical basis functions with optimizable positions, orientations, and scales.

RayGauss associates a combination of spherical harmonics (SH) and spherical Gaussians (SG) with elliptical basis functions to better represent high-frequency color variations such as specular reflections.
RayGauss uses volume ray casting, which produces high-quality images with fewer simplifications than splatting-based methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Splatting algorithms simplify the scene using multiple approximations, allowing faster rendering but causing many artifacts when deviating from the training views, such as flickering due to a sudden change in primitives ordering.

RayGauss introduces a ray casting algorithm for sparse basis functions that sequentially integrates the radiance field slab-by-slab, accumulating colorimetric properties along the ray in slabs of space corresponding to multiple samples.

claim_records.text: NeRFMeshing proposes a novel compact and flexible architecture that enables easy 3D surface reconstruction from any NeRF-driven approach.
NeRFMeshing distills the volumetric 3D representation of a trained radiance field into a Signed Surface Approximation Network, allowing easy extraction of the 3D mesh and appearance.

fact_fields.method: NeRFMeshing distillation into Signed Surface Approximation Network

claim_records.text: The final 3D mesh produced by NeRFMeshing is physically accurate and can be rendered in real time on an array of devices.
NeRFMeshing is an end-to-end pipeline for efficiently extracting geometrically accurate meshes from trained NeRF-based networks, merely adding a very small overhead in time.
NeRFMeshing produces meshes with neural colors having accurate geometry that can be rendered in real time on commodity hardware.

NeRFMeshing introduces a novel signed surface approximation network (SSAN) that produces an accurate 3D triangle mesh of the scene rendered using a small appearance network to produce view-dependent colors.
In contrast to other works that leverage distance fields requiring significant modifications in the used NeRF architecture, NeRFMeshing can be leveraged together with any NeRF.

SSAN estimates a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) and a feature appearance field, harnessing the NeRF approximated geometry as well as the used training views to distill the trained NeRF into the SSAN model.
The 3D mesh extracted from the trained SSAN can be rendered on embedded devices at high frame-rate using rasterization and the appearance network.
NeRFMeshing does not rely on a fixed grid template during training, enabling reconstruction at any arbitrary resolution afterwards.
NeRFMeshing does not require any changes to the NeRF architecture in order to compute a surface.

claims: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.
Optimization of the NeRF representation only requires a set of images with known camera poses as input.
NeRF is parameterized as basic MLP networks to represent continuous scenes with complex geometry and materials as 5D neural radiance fields.
The NeRF differentiable rendering procedure based on classical volume rendering includes a hierarchical sampling strategy to allocate the MLP's capacity towards space with visible scene content.

The basic implementation of optimizing a neural radiance field for a complex scene does not converge to a sufficiently high-resolution representation and is inefficient in the required number of samples per camera ray.
Transforming input 5D coordinates with a positional encoding enables the MLP to represent higher frequency functions.
The proposed hierarchical sampling procedure reduces the number of queries required to adequately sample the high-frequency scene representation.
NeRF overcomes the prohibitive storage costs of discretized voxel grids when modeling complex scenes at high-resolutions.

Ablation studies on the 'Realistic Synthetic 360°' scenes show that positional encoding and view-dependence provide the largest quantitative benefit to NeRF performance, followed by hierarchical sampling.
NeRF's performance using only 25 input images still exceeds NV, SRN, and LLFF across all metrics when those methods are provided with 100 images.

NeRF represents a static scene as a continuous 5D function that outputs radiance emitted in each direction (θ, φ) at each point (x, y, z) in space, plus a density at each point acting like a differential opacity.

NeRF optimizes a deep fully-connected neural network without any convolutional layers (MLP) to regress from a single 5D coordinate (x, y, z, θ, φ) to a single volume density and view-dependent RGB color.

evidence_items.claim_text: The NeRF method represents a scene using a fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network that takes a single continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ, φ)) as input and outputs volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.

fact_fields.method: NeRF scene representation via fully-connected non-convolutional deep network

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF synthesizes novel views by querying 5D coordinates along camera rays and using classic volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities into an image.

fact_fields.method: Classic volume rendering along camera rays

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: Optimization of the NeRF representation only requires a set of images with known camera poses as input.

fact_fields.method: Gradient-based optimization of neural radiance field

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF is parameterized as basic MLP networks to represent continuous scenes with complex geometry and materials as 5D neural radiance fields.

fact_fields.method: 5D neural radiance field parameterized as basic MLP networks

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: The NeRF differentiable rendering procedure based on classical volume rendering includes a hierarchical sampling strategy to allocate the MLP's capacity towards space with visible scene content.

fact_fields.method: Differentiable rendering based on classical volume rendering with hierarchical sampling

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: The basic implementation of optimizing a neural radiance field for a complex scene does not converge to a sufficiently high-resolution representation and is inefficient in the required number of samples per camera ray.

fact_fields.method: Basic neural radiance field optimization without positional encoding or hierarchical sampling

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: Transforming input 5D coordinates with a positional encoding enables the MLP to represent higher frequency functions.

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: The proposed hierarchical sampling procedure reduces the number of queries required to adequately sample the high-frequency scene representation.

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF overcomes the prohibitive storage costs of discretized voxel grids when modeling complex scenes at high-resolutions.

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: Ablation studies on the 'Realistic Synthetic 360°' scenes show that positional encoding and view-dependence provide the largest quantitative benefit to NeRF performance, followed by hierarchical sampling.

fact_fields.method: Ablation study removing components one at a time from the full NeRF model

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF's performance using only 25 input images still exceeds NV, SRN, and LLFF across all metrics when those methods are provided with 100 images.

fact_fields.method: NeRF with reduced input image count

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF represents a static scene as a continuous 5D function that outputs radiance emitted in each direction (θ, φ) at each point (x, y, z) in space, plus a density at each point acting like a differential opacity.

evidence_items.paper_title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
evidence_items.claim_text: NeRF optimizes a deep fully-connected neural network without any convolutional layers (MLP) to regress from a single 5D coordinate (x, y, z, θ, φ) to a single volume density and view-dependent RGB color.

fact_fields.method: Optimization of deep fully-connected MLP without convolutional layers

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF represents the NeRF as a set of polygons with textures representing binary opacities and feature vectors.

MobileNeRF renders polygons with a z-buffer to produce an image with features at every pixel, which are interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP running in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color.

fact_fields.method: Traditional polygon rasterization with z-buffer plus fragment shader MLP

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF achieves interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms, including mobile phones, by using the traditional polygon rasterization pipeline which provides massive pixel-level parallelism.

Traditional NeRF implementations use a volumetric rendering algorithm that evaluates a large MLP at hundreds of sample positions along the ray for each pixel to estimate and integrate density and radiance.
The traditional NeRF volumetric rendering process is far too slow for interactive visualization.
SNeRG's precomputation and deferred rendering approach increases the rendering speed of NeRF by three orders of magnitude.
SNeRG still relies upon ray marching through a sparse voxel grid to produce features for each pixel, and thus cannot fully utilize the parallelism available in commodity GPUs.

fact_fields.method: SNeRG rendering via ray marching through sparse voxel grid

claim_records.text: SNeRG requires a significant amount of GPU memory to store volumetric textures, which prohibits it from running on common mobile devices.
MobileNeRF's rendering pipeline does not sample rays or sort polygons in depth order, and thus can model only binary opacities.
MobileNeRF is 10× faster than SNeRG with the same output quality on standard test scenes.
MobileNeRF consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures, enabling it to run on integrated GPUs with limited memory and power.

fact_fields.method: MobileNeRF surface texture storage vs volumetric texture storage

claim_records.text: MobileNeRF runs on a web browser and is compatible with all devices tested, as its viewer is an HTML webpage.
MobileNeRF allows real-time manipulation of reconstructed objects/scenes, as they are simple triangle meshes.
MobileNeRF does not need reconstructed 3D geometry as input.
Rendering a NeRF involves evaluating a large neural network at multiple 3D locations per pixel, preventing real-time rendering.

claim_records.text: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic distillation method that allows any-to-any conversions between different NeRF architectures, including MLP, sparse or low-rank tensors, hashtables and their compositions.
PVD performs distillation progressively on different levels of volume representations, from shallower to deeper, to enable fast conversions.
PVD employs special treatment of density to address its specific numerical instability problem.
Empirical validation of PVD is conducted on the NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF and TanksAndTemples datasets.

With PVD, an MLP-based NeRF model can be distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model at a 10X~20X faster speed than training the original NeRF from scratch, while achieving a superior level of synthesis quality.
Hashtable-based NeRF representations admit faster training and rendering but their lack of clear geometric meaning hampers downstream tasks like spatial-relation-aware editing.
PVD empowers downstream applications to optimally adapt neural representations for the task at hand in a post hoc fashion.

A NeRF model distilled by PVD from an INGP teacher within 1.5 hours achieves improved synthesis quality and reduces training time compared to a NeRF trained from scratch using 25 hours on the Family and Barn scene from the TanksAndTemples dataset.
TensoRF leverages VM (vector-matrix) decomposition and canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) to produce compact feature tensor representations.
Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (INGP) utilizes multilevel hash tables for effective compression of feature tensors.
Implicit NeRF representations make texture editing of scenes (such as color, lighting changes and deformations) easier, to the extent of artistic stylization and dynamic scene modeling.

Methods with explicit or hybrid NeRF representations usually enjoy faster training due to shallower representations and cope better with geometric-aware editing like merging and other manipulations of scenes.
PVD offers any-to-any conversion between possibly heterogeneous NeRF architectures by first constructing a unified view of them, then employing systematic progressive distillation in multiple stages.
PVD employs a special treatment of the dynamic density volume range by clipping, which improves training stability and significantly improves synthesis quality.
Distillation from hashtable and VM-decomposition structures often either helps boost student model synthesis quality and consumes less time than training from scratch.
PVD builds a block-wise distillation strategy to accelerate the training procedure based on a unified view of different NeRF architectures.

When a teacher model with hash table is used to distill a student model of explicit representation, it is possible to benefit from the faster training speed of the teacher while still producing a student model with clear geometric structures.

claim_records.text: NeRF generates a volumetric representation called a radiance field, which is capable of creating color and density for every point within the relevant 3D space, rather than directly restoring the whole 3D scene geometry.
NeRF leverages an interpolation approach to produce new 3D reconstructed views of complicated scenes.
This survey reviews recent advances in NeRF and categorizes them according to their architectural designs, especially in the field of novel view synthesis.
CAMPARI simultaneously learns a camera generator and an image generator, enabling use of complex camera distributions without manual tuning.
CAMPARI represents scenes efficiently through foreground and background decomposition, leading to 3D-consistent representations and accurate camera distribution recovery.
CAMPARI surpasses baseline models which heavily depend on accurately matched camera distributions, due to its performance without camera parameter tuning.
CAMPARI faces the challenge of generating inward-facing faces compared to the traditional inverted faces also known as the hollow face illusion where convex faces appear concave.
Pix2NeRF introduces a novel pipeline to generate NeRF from a single input image, building upon π-GAN, a 3D image synthesis generative model that maps latent codes to radiance fields.
Pix2NeRF employs an unsupervised approach and can be trained with independent images, offering potential applications in 3D avatar generation, novel view synthesis, and super-resolution.
A limitation of Pix2NeRF is its current restriction to work with only one category per dataset, impeding its ability to generalize to new categories.
Pix2NeRF is built on top of π-GAN but is not limited to using π-GAN as its backbone; newer generative NeRF models such as EG3D may achieve better visual quality if used as a backbone.

NeRF uses a deep neural network to represent complex scenes in a fully connected, non-convolutional way, with input as a continuous 5D coordinate and output as volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance at that spatial location.
The 5D coordinate space for NeRF includes three dimensions for spatial coordinates (x,y,z) and two dimensions for camera viewing angles (θ,φ).
NeRF uses classic volume rendering techniques to synthesize views and is optimized using a set of images with known camera poses.
NeRF introduces a positional encoding and a hierarchical sampling strategy to address the inefficiency of the basic implementation.
Using input viewing direction, NeRF can represent non-Lambertian effects such as specularities.
NeRF uses a separate neural continuous volume representation network for each scene.

claim_records.text: The introduced single-view volumetric field reconstruction technique is designed for volumes where multiple light scattering effects are omnipresent, such as clouds.
The unknown distribution of volumetric fields is modeled using an unconditional diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset of 1,000 synthetically simulated volumetric density fields.
The neural diffusion model is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly, monoplanar representation.
A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space.

The proposed approach's use of a physically-based differentiable volume renderer for latent-space light transport gradients makes reconstructions better aligned with observed data, in contrast to classic NeRF approaches.

fact_fields.method: physically-based differentiable volume renderer coupled with diffusion model

claim_records.text: Experiments demonstrate single-view reconstruction of volumetric clouds at a previously unattainable quality.

Reconstructing the internal density distribution of highly dense volumes is nearly impossible due to high uncertainty in the light scattering process and the presence of vanishing gradients, and this limitation can only be alleviated by incorporating prior information during reconstruction.

For complex volumetric materials such as clouds, smoke, or fire, the reconstruction problem is so ill-posed that it requires dozens, if not hundreds, of different views to adequately constrain object parameters.
Using diffusion models for single-view volume reconstruction is challenging because no publicly available 3D dataset exists on which a diffusion model can be trained.
The proposed approach employs a diffusion prior to guide a Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR) toward reconstructing a plausible volumetric field.

fact_fields.method: diffusion prior guided Physically-based Differentiable Volume Renderer (PDVR)

The reconstruction is simultaneously constrained by the diffusion prior and the image containing light transport effects.

claim_records.text: Hyb-NeRF is a novel neural radiance field with a multi-resolution hybrid encoding that achieves efficient neural modeling and fast rendering, while also allowing for high-quality novel view synthesis.
Hyb-NeRF represents the scene using different encoding strategies from coarse-to-fine resolution levels.
Hyb-NeRF exploits memory-efficient learnable positional features at coarse resolutions and the fast optimization speed and local details of hash-based feature grids at fine resolutions.
Hyb-NeRF embeds cone tracing-based features in its learnable positional encoding, which eliminates encoding ambiguity and reduces aliasing artifacts.

claim_records.text: On a challenging multiresolution benchmark, mip-NeRF reduces error rates relative to NeRF by 60% on average.
Mip-NeRF is slightly faster than NeRF by approximately 7%.
Mip-NeRF has half as many parameters as NeRF.
IPE preserves frequencies that are constant over an interval and softly removes frequencies that vary over an interval, while PE preserves all frequencies up to a manually-tuned hyperparameter L.
IPE removes L as a hyperparameter, which can be set to an extremely large value and never tuned.
Mip-NeRF uses a single MLP with parameters Θ, repeatedly queried in a hierarchical sampling strategy, instead of NeRF's separate coarse and fine MLPs.
Mip-NeRF matches the accuracy of a brute-force supersampled NeRF on the multiscale dataset while being 22× faster.
NeRF casts a single ray through each pixel and queries an MLP for scene properties at samples along that ray, then composites values into a single color.

Mip-NeRF reasons about the 3D conical frustum defined by a camera pixel, featurized with integrated positional encoding (IPE) by approximating the frustum with a multivariate Gaussian and computing the closed-form integral E[γ(x)] over positional encodings of coordinates within the Gaussian.
NeRF trains two separate MLPs, one coarse and one fine, with parameters Θc and Θf to improve sample efficiency.
NeRF training minimizes the sum of squared differences between all input pixel values and all predicted pixel values using gradient descent.

claim_records.text: NerfDiff distills knowledge of a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) into NeRF by synthesizing and refining a set of virtual views at test time.
NerfDiff significantly outperforms existing NeRF-based and geometry-free approaches on the ShapeNet, ABO, and Clevr3D datasets.
NerfDiff jointly trains a camera-space triplane-based NeRF together with a 3D-aware conditional diffusion model (CDM) on a collection of scenes at the training stage.
A naive finetuning strategy that optimizes NeRF parameters directly using CDM outputs leads to subpar renderings because CDM outputs tend to be multi-view inconsistent.

fact_fields.method: naive NeRF finetuning using CDM outputs

claim_records.text: NerfDiff's NeRF-guided distillation updates the NeRF representation and guides the multi-view diffusion process in an alternating fashion.
NerfDiff introduces an efficient image-conditioned NeRF representation based on camera-aligned triplanes that enables efficient rendering and finetuning from the CDM.
NerfDiff's 3D-aware CDM integrates volume rendering into 2D diffusion models to facilitate generalization to novel views.
Generalizable NeRF models conditioned by projecting 3D points and gathering corresponding image features produce blurry results when target views are far from the input view.

fact_fields.method: generalizable NeRF models conditioned on projected 3D point image features

claim_records.text: EvaSurf can be trained in 1-2 hours using a single GPU.
EvaSurf can run on mobile devices at over 40 FPS.
The final rendering package required for EvaSurf takes up only 40-50 MB of storage.
EvaSurf employs an efficient surface-based model with a multi-view supervision module to ensure accurate mesh reconstruction.
EvaSurf learns an implicit texture embedded with a set of Gaussian lobes to capture view-dependent information for high-fidelity rendering.
EvaSurf uses a lightweight neural shader paired with explicit geometry and implicit texture to reduce computation cost and support real-time rendering on common mobile devices.
EvaSurf can reconstruct high-quality appearance and accurate mesh on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
EvaSurf's training procedure is 10× faster than MobileNeRF when completed on a single GPU.

claim_records.text: NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 22.77 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 20.85.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.823 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 0.747.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.298 on the Truck scene, compared to NeRF's 0.513.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 17.17 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 16.64.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.672 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 0.635.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.523 on the Train scene, compared to NeRF's 0.651.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 17.88 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 16.86.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.738 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 0.702.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.435 on the M60 scene, compared to NeRF's 0.602.
NeRF++ achieves a PSNR of 22.37 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 21.55.
NeRF++ achieves an SSIM of 0.799 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 0.765.
NeRF++ achieves an LPIPS of 0.391 on the Playground scene, compared to NeRF's 0.529.
NeRF++ uses twice the number of samples per camera ray compared to a single volume NeRF, doubling NeRF's sample count for fairness.

For outdoor 360-degree captures centered on nearby objects, the dynamic depth range can be extremely large because background elements such as buildings, mountains, and clouds can be arbitrarily far away.
NeRF++ partitions scene space into an inner unit sphere containing foreground and all cameras, and an outer volume represented by an inverted sphere covering the complement of the inner volume.

In theory, optimizing NeRF's 5D radiance function from a set of training images can encounter critical degenerate solutions that fail to generalize to novel test views in the absence of regularization.
The shape-radiance ambiguity allows fitting a set of training images perfectly for an arbitrary incorrect geometry by choosing a suitable outgoing 2D radiance at each surface point.
NeRF's specific MLP structure implicitly encodes a smooth BRDF prior on surface reflectance, which helps avoid shape-radiance ambiguity.
A shape-radiance ambiguity solution that perfectly fits training images has very limited ability to synthesize novel views unless training views are extremely dense.

claim_records.text: NeRF yields blurred rendering results when training images are captured at non-uniform scales.
NeRF produces aliasing artifacts when test images are taken from distant views.
Mip-NeRF uses a conical frustum multiscale representation with integrated positional encoding (IPE) to query an MLP, making it only suitable for offline rendering.
Mip-VoG is an explicit multiscale representation with a deferred architecture designed for real-time anti-aliasing rendering.
Mip-VoG encodes scene scale using the level of detail (LOD) derived from ray differentials.
Mip-VoG uses quadrilinear interpolation to map a queried 3D location to its features and density from two neighboring downsampled voxel grids.
Mip-VoG is claimed to be the first approach to offer multiscale training and real-time anti-aliasing rendering simultaneously.
Experiments on multiscale datasets show that Mip-VoG outperforms state-of-the-art real-time rendering baselines.

claim_records.text: pixelNeRF outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines for novel view synthesis and single image 3D reconstruction when demonstrated on multi-object ShapeNet scenes and real scenes from the DTU dataset.
NeRF represents a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field f that maps a 3D point x and viewing direction unit vector d to a differential density σ and RGB color c.
NeRF renders a 2D image from its volumetric radiance field via the integral Ĉ(r) = ∫_{tn}^{tf} T(t)σ(t)c(t)dt, where T(t) = exp(−∫_{tn}^{t} σ(s) ds) handles occlusion.

In the single-view pixelNeRF case, for a query point x along a target camera ray with view direction d, a corresponding image feature is extracted from the feature volume W via projection and interpolation, then passed into the NeRF network along with spatial coordinates to produce volume-rendered output compared against the target pixel value.

For multi-view pixelNeRF, the query point x and view direction d are transformed into each input view i's coordinate system via x(i) = P(i)x, d(i) = R(i)d, processed independently by initial NeRF layers f1, then aggregated via average pooling ψ and passed to final layers f2 to produce predicted density and color.
pixelNeRF is applied to new scenes immediately without any test-time optimization, whereas running each of 60 NeRFs took 14 hours.
pixelNeRF's rendering time increases linearly when given more input views, similar to NeRF's slow rendering time.
pixelNeRF manually tunes ray sampling bounds tn, tf and a scale for the positional encoding, as in vanilla NeRF.
pixelNeRF's approach is bottlenecked by the availability of large-scale wide baseline multi-view datasets, limiting its applicability to datasets such as ShapeNet and DTU.

claim_records.text: CLIP-NeRF is a multi-modal 3D object manipulation method for neural radiance fields that leverages the joint language-image embedding space of the CLIP model to enable NeRF manipulation using either a short text prompt or an exemplar image.

CLIP-NeRF uses a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture that allows individual control over both shape and appearance, achieved by performing shape conditioning via a learned deformation field applied to positional encoding and deferring color conditioning to the volumetric rendering stage.
CLIP-NeRF designs two code mappers that take a CLIP embedding as input and update latent codes to reflect targeted editing, trained with a CLIP-based matching loss to ensure manipulation accuracy.
CLIP-NeRF proposes an inverse optimization method that accurately projects an input image to latent codes to enable editing on real images.
CLIP-NeRF provides an intuitive interface for interactive editing, evaluated via extensive experiments on a variety of text prompts and exemplar images.

claim_records.text: UE4-NeRF partitions each large scene into different sub-NeRFs to support real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.
UE4-NeRF initializes polygonal meshes by constructing multiple regular octahedra within the scene, with vertices of the polygonal faces continuously optimized during training.

claim_records.text: D-NeRF extends neural radiance fields to dynamic domains, enabling reconstruction and rendering of novel images of objects under rigid and non-rigid motions from a single moving camera around the scene.

D-NeRF splits learning into two simultaneous fully-connected network stages: one encoding the scene into canonical space, and another mapping the canonical representation to the deformed scene at a particular time.

D-NeRF's Deformation Network Ψt is trained to output displacement ∆x that transforms a given 3D point x at time t to its canonical space position as x + ∆x, with the canonical scene set to t=0 such that Ψt(x,0)=0.
D-NeRF uses positional encoder γ(p)=<(sin(2^l π p), cos(2^l π p))>_{L=0}^L, with L=10 for spatial coordinate x and L=4 for view direction d and time t.
D-NeRF's Canonical Network is an MLP Ψx(x,d) that maps a 3D point x and view direction d to emitted color c and volume density σ in canonical configuration.
D-NeRF's Deformation Network is an MLP Ψt(x,t) that predicts a deformation field defining the transformation between the scene at time t and its canonical configuration.
D-NeRF can learn a volumetric density representation for continuous non-rigid scenes trained with a single view per time instant.

For D-NeRF volume rendering, the expected pixel color C(p,t) at time t is computed as C(p,t)=∫_{hn}^{hf} T(h,t)σ(p(h,t))c(p(h,t),d) dh, where p(h,t)=x(h)+Ψt(x(h,t)), [c,σ]=Ψx(p(h,t),d), and T(h,t)=exp(-∫_{hn}^h σ(p(s,t)) ds).

D-NeRF evaluation on its 8 dynamic scenes uses four metrics: Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS).
Baseline NeRF, designed for rigid scenes, fails to model dynamic scenes and converges to a blurry mean representation of all deformations.
T-NeRF baseline, which represents the scene as a 6D input (x,y,z,θ,φ,t) without intermediate canonical configuration, captures dynamics reasonably well but fails to retrieve high frequency details.
D-NeRF retains high-frequency original image details in novel views even when each deformation state is only observed from a single viewpoint.

D-NeRF learns a displacement field ∆x mapping all points x of a dynamic scene at a specific time to a common canonical configuration, with learned volume density and view-dependent radiance transferred back to input points for novel view rendering.

claim_records.text: NeRF's novel view synthesis performance drops significantly when the number of input training views is reduced.
The majority of artifacts in sparse-input NeRF scenarios are caused by errors in estimated scene geometry and divergent behavior at the start of training.
RegNeRF addresses sparse-input NeRF artifacts by regularizing geometry and appearance of patches rendered from unobserved viewpoints, and annealing the ray sampling space during training.
RegNeRF additionally uses a normalizing flow model to regularize the color of unobserved viewpoints.
RegNeRF outperforms other single-scene optimization methods, and in many cases also outperforms conditional models extensively pre-trained on large multi-view datasets.

claim_records.text: The proposed voxel grid optimization approach converges rapidly from scratch in less than 15 minutes with a single GPU while achieving NeRF-comparable quality.
Evaluation on five inward-facing benchmarks shows the method matches, if not surpasses, NeRF's quality, yet it only takes about 15 minutes to train from scratch for a new scene.
The method with 160^3 dense voxels already outperforms NeRF in most cases.
Using softplus instead of ReLU is crucial to optimize voxel density directly, as it allows exploring density very close to 0.
The proposed post-activation can model (beyond) a sharp linear surface within a single grid cell.
The step-size-to-voxel-size ratio is an important hyperparameter for the speed-quality tradeoff.
Progressive scaling of voxel grid resolution in fine-stage training can improve training efficiency with slightly better rendering quality.

claim_records.text: ProteusNeRF is a neural network architecture for NeRF editing that is fast, efficient, and maintains a low memory footprint.
ProteusNeRF supports incremental guidance through user-friendly image-based edits.
ProteusNeRF enables straightforward object selection via semantic feature distillation at the training stage.
ProteusNeRF uses a local 3D-aware image context to facilitate view-consistent image editing that can then be distilled into fine-tuned NeRFs via geometric and appearance adjustments.
ProteusNeRF reports a 10-30x speedup over concurrent work focusing on text-guided NeRF editing.

claim_records.text: Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) models the radiance distribution along each ray with frequency basis and predicts frequency weights using the network, with pixel values computed via volume rendering on radiance distributions.
NeRDF uses a small network similar to NeRF while preserving rendering speed with a single network forwarding per pixel as in Neural Light Fields.
NeRDF achieves a ~254x speed-up over NeRF with similar network size, with only a marginal performance decline.
NeRDF offers a better trade-off among speed, quality, and network size than existing methods.

claim_records.text: VQ-NeRF uses a multi-scale NeRF sampling scheme that concurrently optimizes the NeRF model at both compressed and original scales to enhance the network's ability to preserve fine details.
VQ-NeRF incorporates a semantic loss function to improve the geometric fidelity and semantic coherence of 3D reconstructions.

Recent works that include alternative sampling approaches to help accelerate NeRF methods often do not focus on the sampling approach itself.

claim_records.text: Current 3D representations including meshes, voxels, point clouds, and NeRF-based neural implicit fields are often task-specific and lack universal applicability across reconstruction, generation, editing, and driving.
Meshes offer high precision but their dense vertex data complicates editing.
NeRFs deliver excellent rendering but suffer from structural ambiguity, hindering animation and manipulation.
All existing 3D representations inherently struggle with the trade-off between data complexity and fidelity.

The 3D Hierarchical Proxy Node representation represents an object's shape and texture via a sparse set of hierarchically organized tree-structured proxy nodes distributed on its surface and interior.
Each proxy node stores local shape and texture information implicitly encoded by a small MLP within its neighborhood.
Querying any 3D coordinate's properties involves efficient neural interpolation and lightweight decoding from relevant nearby and parent nodes.

The Hierarchical Proxy Node framework yields a highly compact representation where nodes align with local semantics, enabling direct drag-and-edit manipulation and offering scalable quality-complexity control.
Extensive experiments across 3D reconstruction and editing demonstrate the HPR3D method's expressive efficiency, high-fidelity rendering quality, and superior editability.
